But his professional and scientific ambitions mattered to those advantages no more, in her eyes, than a lucky discovery of some foul-smelling oil might have done. Apart from that oil, which was none of her concern, she naturally trusted her own judgment more than his. In countless small matters, as well as in the serious affair of riding, Lydgate was astonished that affection did not make her obedient. He did not doubt her affection or suspect he had done anything to repel it. He told himself that he loved her as tenderly as ever and could accept the things she would not give him. And yet—well, he was deeply troubled. He felt new elements entering his life, as poisonous to him as an inflow of mud to a creature accustomed to breathing, bathing, and darting after sunlit prey in the clearest water.

Soon Rosamond looked lovelier than ever at her worktable. She enjoyed drives in her father's phaeton and thought an invitation to Quallingham likely. She knew she would adorn its drawing room more exquisitely than any daughter of the family. In reflecting that the gentlemen knew it too, she perhaps did not sufficiently consider whether the ladies would be eager to see themselves outshone.

Freed from anxiety about her health, Lydgate fell back into what she privately called his moodiness. For her, the term covered both his thoughtful absorption in matters other than herself and the genuinely troubled brow and distaste for ordinary things—as though everything were flavored with bitter herbs—that served as a barometer of his distress and forebodings. One cause among others of this distress was something he had generously but mistakenly withheld from Rosamond, fearing for her health and spirits. Husband and wife completely missed the path of each other's thoughts, something all too plainly possible even in people constantly thinking about one another. To Lydgate, it seemed that for month after month his tenderness toward her had consumed more than half his best intentions and energies. He had borne her little demands and interruptions patiently. Above all, without revealing bitterness, he had endured seeing her mind's blank, unreflective surface ever more clearly as his illusions thinned away. It offered nothing to his passion for the impersonal purposes of his profession and scientific study—a passion he had supposed the ideal wife would somehow worship as sublime, without understanding why. But his endurance was mixed with dissatisfaction with himself. If we are honest, we will admit that this supplies more than half the bitterness we feel about our grievances, including those involving a wife or husband. It remains true that if we had been greater, circumstances would have had less power against us. Lydgate knew that his concessions to Rosamond were often little more than a weakening of resolve: the creeping paralysis that can seize an enthusiasm at odds with a permanent part of one's life. And what continually pressed upon his enthusiasm was not simply sorrow, but the gnawing presence of a petty, humiliating worry, the kind that casts a blighting irony over every higher effort.

This was the worry he had so far kept from Rosamond. To his surprise, he believed it had never entered her mind, although nothing could have been less mysterious. The conclusion had an obvious handle, easily grasped even by casual observers: Lydgate was in debt. He could not keep from thinking for long that every day drew him deeper into that swamp, which lures men with such a lovely surface of flowers and greenery. It is astonishing how quickly a man finds himself up to his chin. Then, against his will, escape becomes his chief concern, even if his soul once held a plan of the universe.

Eighteen months earlier, Lydgate had been poor without ever knowing the urgent need for small sums. He had felt a burning contempt for anyone who stooped to obtain them. Now he suffered something worse than an ordinary shortfall: the vulgar, hateful troubles of a man who has bought and used many unnecessary things, cannot pay for them, and faces increasingly insistent demands.

It takes little arithmetic or knowledge of prices to see how this happened. A man setting up house and preparing to marry spends four or five hundred pounds more on furnishings and initial costs than his capital can cover. At the year's end, household expenses, horses, and the rest amount to nearly a thousand. Meanwhile, a medical practice that the old accounts valued at eight hundred pounds a year has shrunk like a pond in summer and scarcely brings in five hundred, mostly in unpaid bills. The obvious conclusion is that, whether he concerns himself with it or not, he is in debt. Living cost less then than it does in our own time, and provincial habits were comparatively modest. Still, anyone willing to consider the details can see how easily a doctor who had recently bought a practice, thought two horses essential, kept a plentiful table, paid life insurance, and rented an expensive house and garden could find his spending double his income. Brought up in an extravagant home, Rosamond assumed good housekeeping meant ordering the best of everything. Nothing else “did the job.” Lydgate believed that “if things are done at all, they must be done properly.” He could not see how else they could live. Had each category of household spending been put before him in advance, he would probably have said it “could hardly amount to much.” A suggestion of economizing on a particular item—buying inexpensive fish instead of costly fish, for instance—would have struck him as mere penny-pinching meanness. Rosamond liked inviting guests even without an occasion such as Captain Lydgate's visit. Though Lydgate often found them tedious, he did not interfere. Such sociability seemed a necessary professional precaution, and the entertainment had to be appropriate. It is true that he constantly visited poor people's homes and tailored his dietary prescriptions to their limited means. But dear me, surely we no longer find it remarkable that men can keep many strands of experience side by side without ever comparing them. Do we not rather expect it? Spending, like ugliness or mistakes, becomes an entirely different thing when we attach ourselves to it and judge it by the enormous difference we feel between ourselves and other people. Lydgate thought himself indifferent to clothes. He despised a man who calculated the impression his outfit would make. To him, having abundant fresh clothing was simply natural; one ordered such things by the bundle. Remember that he had never before been checked by persistent creditors. He followed habit rather than self-examination. Now the check had come.

Its unfamiliarity made it more galling. He was amazed and disgusted that conditions so alien to his purposes, so hatefully unrelated to the things he cared to work on, could have lain waiting and seized him unawares. Nor was there only the existing debt. In his present circumstances, he was certain to keep adding to it. Two Brassing furnishing tradesmen, whom he had owed money since before his marriage, had repeatedly sent unpleasant letters that forced themselves upon his attention. Unplanned everyday expenses had prevented him from paying them all this time. Few temperaments could have found this more painful than Lydgate's, with his fierce pride and aversion to asking favors or owing obligations. He had scorned even to speculate about Mr. Vincy's financial intentions. Only extreme need could have driven him to apply to his father-in-law, even without the various indirect signs since his marriage that Mr. Vincy's own business was struggling and that any expectation of assistance would be resented. Some men readily trust that friends will help. Earlier in life, Lydgate had never imagined needing to rely on that. He had never considered what borrowing would feel like. Now that the idea had entered his mind, he felt he would rather endure any other hardship. Meanwhile, he had neither money nor prospects of money, and his practice was not becoming more profitable.

It was hardly surprising that in recent months Lydgate had failed to conceal every sign of inner distress. Now that Rosamond's excellent health was returning, he considered taking her fully into his confidence. His new familiarity with tradesmen's bills had driven his reasoning into fresh comparisons. He had begun to reconsider which purchases were necessary and which were not, and to recognize that their habits must change. How could they change without Rosamond's cooperation? The immediate occasion for disclosing the unpleasant facts was forced on him.

With no money available, Lydgate had privately sought advice about what security a man in his position could offer. He then proposed the one solid guarantee within his power to the less demanding of his creditors, a silversmith and jeweler. This man agreed to take over the debt to the upholsterer too, receiving interest for a fixed period. The required security was a bill of sale giving rights over the household furniture. That might reassure a creditor for a reasonable time about a debt of less than four hundred pounds. The silversmith, Mr. Dover, was also willing to lower the debt by taking back some of the silver and any other item still as good as new. “Any other item” delicately meant jewelry, especially the purple amethysts costing thirty pounds that Lydgate had bought as a wedding present.

There may be different views about the wisdom of that present. Some may consider it a graceful gesture to be expected from a man like Lydgate. They may blame any troublesome consequences on the cramped conditions of provincial life at the time, which offered no convenient arrangements for professional men whose fortunes did not match their tastes. They may also blame Lydgate's absurd scruples about asking friends for money.

On the fine morning when he went to place a final order for silver, however, the question had seemed unimportant. Beside jewels of enormous price, and added to orders whose total he had never precisely calculated, thirty pounds for ornaments so perfectly suited to Rosamond's neck and arms could hardly seem excessive when there was no available cash to exceed. Now, in this crisis, he could not stop imagining the amethysts returned to Mr. Dover's stock, though he recoiled from suggesting it to Rosamond. Awakened to consequences he had never habitually traced, he was preparing to act on that new understanding with some—by no means all—of the rigor he would bring to an experiment. Riding home from Brassing, he braced himself for such firmness and considered how to explain matters to her.

He arrived home in the evening. This gifted, vigorous man of twenty-nine was profoundly miserable. He was not angrily telling himself he had made a terrible mistake; but the mistake worked within him like a chronic disease he knew he had. Its discomfort intruded into every prospect and weakened every thought. Walking down the passage toward the drawing room, he heard singing and the piano. Of course, Ladislaw was there. Several weeks had passed since Will said goodbye to Dorothea, yet he still occupied his old place in Middlemarch. Usually Lydgate had no objection to his visits. Just now, he resented not finding his own fireside free. When he opened the door, the two singers continued toward the final keynote. They looked up at him but did not regard his arrival as an interruption. For a man chafed by his harness as poor Lydgate was, coming home with the knowledge that a painful day still held more pain, the sight of two people warbling at him was no comfort. His already unusually pale face darkened into a scowl as he crossed the room and threw himself into a chair.
The singers, considering themselves excused because only three bars had remained, now turned around.
“How are you, Lydgate?” Will asked, coming forward to shake his hand.
Lydgate shook hands but did not consider a spoken reply necessary.
“Have you eaten, Tertius? I thought you'd be back much sooner,” Rosamond said, taking her usual seat. She had already noticed that her husband was in a “horrible mood.”
“I've eaten. I'd like some tea, please,” Lydgate said shortly. Still scowling, he stared pointedly at his legs stretched before him.
Will understood at once. “I'll be going,” he said, reaching for his hat.
“The tea will be here soon,” Rosamond said. “Please stay.”
“No, Lydgate's out of sorts,” Will replied. He understood Lydgate better than Rosamond did, and took no offense at his manner, readily imagining annoyances outside the house.
“All the more reason for you to stay,” Rosamond said playfully, in her lightest voice. “He won't speak to me all evening.”
“Yes, Rosamond, I will,” Lydgate said in his strong baritone. “There's serious business I need to discuss with you.”
He could hardly have introduced the subject in a way less like the one he had planned. But her indifference had provoked him beyond endurance.
“There, you see,” Will said. “I'm off to the meeting about the Mechanics' Institute. Goodbye.” He quickly left the room.

Rosamond did not look at her husband. After a moment she rose and sat before the tea tray, thinking she had never seen him so disagreeable. Lydgate watched with dark eyes as her tapered fingers delicately handled the tea things. She looked only at the objects immediately before her. Not a line of her face was disturbed, yet her manner expressed an indescribable protest against everyone with unpleasant manners. For a moment he forgot his own hurt in sudden speculation about this unfamiliar kind of feminine imperturbability. It was revealing itself in the delicate figure he had once taken as a sign of responsive intelligence and feeling. Looking at Rosamond, his mind went back to Laure. “Would _she_ kill me because I bored her?” he wondered; then, “All women are like this.” But this gift for generalization, which gives men such a superiority in error over animals that cannot speak, was immediately checked by his memory of another woman. He remembered his astonishment at Dorothea's behavior: her looks and emotional voice when he first attended her husband; her passionate plea to be told what would comfort that man, for whose sake she seemed obliged to silence every impulse except the longings of loyalty and compassion. While the tea brewed, these memories passed rapidly and dreamily through Lydgate's mind. In the final moment of his reverie he closed his eyes and heard Dorothea saying, “Advise me. Think what I can do. He's spent his whole life working and looking forward. Nothing else matters to him—and nothing else matters to me.”

That deeply feeling woman's voice had stayed with him like the inspiring ideas of dead masters of genius. Is there not also a genius for noble feeling that rules human minds and their judgments? Her tones were music from which he was drifting away. He had actually dozed for a moment when Rosamond said in her silvery, neutral voice, “Your tea, Tertius.” She placed it on the little table beside him, then returned to her seat without looking at him. Lydgate was too quick to judge her unfeeling. In her own way she was quite sensitive, and impressions lasted. Now she felt offended and repelled. But Rosamond never scowled and had never raised her voice. She was entirely certain no one could fairly blame her.

Perhaps they had never felt so distant from one another. Yet there were strong reasons not to delay the disclosure, even if he had not already begun it with that abrupt announcement. Indeed, mixed with his distress at the pain he expected to cause her was some of the angry wish to make her feel more for him that had made him speak too soon. Still, he waited until the tray had been removed, candles lit, and the evening's quiet could be relied on. The interval gave his rejected tenderness time to return to its old course. He spoke kindly.
“Dear Rosy, put your work down and come sit beside me,” he said softly. He pushed the table aside and reached to draw a chair close to his.

Rosamond came. In her drapery of sheer, faintly colored muslin, her slender yet rounded figure had never looked more graceful. She sat beside him, rested one hand on the arm of his chair, and finally looked up to meet his eyes. Her delicate neck and cheek and finely shaped lips had never shown more of that unspoiled beauty which moves us in spring, in infancy, and in everything sweet and fresh. It moved Lydgate now, mingling the earliest moments of his love with all the other memories stirred by this deep crisis. He gently laid his broad hand over hers and said:

“Dear!” He lingered over the word as affection does. Rosamond too still felt the power of their shared past. Her husband was still partly the Lydgate whose approval had delighted her. She lightly brushed his hair away from his forehead, then placed her other hand on his, conscious of forgiving him.
“Rosy, I have to tell you something that will hurt you. But there are matters husband and wife must consider together. I expect you've already realized I'm short of money.”
He paused. Rosamond turned her head and looked at a vase on the mantel.

“I couldn't pay for everything we needed before the wedding. Since then, there have been other expenses I've had to meet. As a result, I owe a large amount in Brassing—three hundred and eighty pounds. It's been weighing on me for some time. In fact we're sinking further into debt each day, because people don't pay me sooner simply because someone else needs the money. I tried hard to keep it from you while you were unwell. Now we must face it together, and you must help me.”

“What can _I_ do, Tertius?” Rosamond turned her eyes back toward him. Those four little words, like so many phrases in every language, can convey through different tones any state of mind: from helpless bewilderment to complete argumentative understanding, from devoted partnership to utter detachment. Rosamond's thin voice filled “What can—I—do!” with all the detachment it could hold. The words struck a deathly chill into Lydgate's newly awakened tenderness. He did not explode in anger; his heart sank too painfully for that. When he spoke again, he sounded more like a man forcing himself to complete a task.
“You need to know because I must provide security for a time. A man has to come and list the furniture.”
Rosamond flushed deeply. As soon as she could speak, she asked, “Haven't you asked Papa for money?”
“I haven't.”
“Then I must!” She withdrew her hands from his and stood up, putting two yards between them.

“No, Rosy,” Lydgate said firmly. “It's too late for that. They'll begin the inventory tomorrow. Remember, it's only security. It won't change anything. It's temporary.” Then he added more insistently, “Your father is not to know unless I choose to tell him.”

That was certainly unkind. But Rosamond had revived his worst expectations of her quiet, unwavering disobedience. To her, his unkindness seemed unforgivable. She disliked crying and seldom did, but now her lips and chin trembled and tears rose. Perhaps, under the combined pressure of material difficulties and his proud resistance to their humiliating consequences, Lydgate could not fully imagine what this sudden ordeal meant to a young woman who had known only indulgence and dreamed of fresh indulgence, more precisely suited to her taste. Yet he wanted to spare her as much as possible, and her tears pierced him. For a moment he could not speak. Rosamond did not continue sobbing. She tried to master her agitation, wiped away the tears, and kept looking straight ahead at the mantel.

“Try not to be so distressed, darling,” Lydgate said, looking up at her. Her choice to move away from him in this moment of trouble made everything harder to say, but he absolutely had to continue. “We must prepare ourselves to do what's needed. I've been at fault. I should have realized we couldn't afford to live like this. But many things have gone against me in the practice, and just now it's at a very low ebb. I may build it up again. Meanwhile, we must stop short and change how we live. We'll get through this. Once I've given the security, I'll have time to consider what to do. You're so clever that if you apply yourself to managing, you'll teach me to be careful. I've been a thoughtless scoundrel about making the figures add up. But come, dear, sit down and forgive me.”

Lydgate bent his neck under the yoke like a creature equipped with claws but also with Reason, which so often makes us meek. At his last pleading words, Rosamond returned to the chair beside him. His self-reproach gave her some hope that he might listen to her opinion. She said:
“Why can't you postpone the inventory? When the men arrive tomorrow, you can send them away.”
“I won't send them away,” Lydgate said, his commanding tone returning. Would explaining do any good?
“If we left Middlemarch, we'd naturally sell everything. That would serve just as well.”
“But we're not leaving Middlemarch.”
“I'm certain it would be far better, Tertius. Why can't we go to London? Or somewhere near Durham, where your family is known?”
“Without money, Rosamond, we can't go anywhere.”
“Your friends wouldn't want you to be left without money. Surely these horrid tradesmen could be made to understand that and wait, if you explained the situation properly.”

“This is pointless, Rosamond,” Lydgate said angrily. “You must learn to trust my judgment in matters you don't understand. I've made the arrangements that are necessary, and they'll be carried out. As for friends, I expect nothing from them and won't ask them for anything.”
Rosamond sat without moving. She was thinking that if she had known how Lydgate would behave, she would never have married him.

“We haven't time to waste on unnecessary talk, dear,” Lydgate said, trying again to be gentle. “I need to discuss a few details with you. Dover will take back quite a lot of the silver, and any jewelry we choose to return. He's really behaving very well.”

“Are we supposed to manage without spoons and forks, then?” Rosamond asked. Even her lips seemed to grow thinner with the thinness of her voice. She had decided to offer no further resistance or suggestions.

“Of course not, dear,” Lydgate said. “But look.” He took a paper from his pocket and unfolded it. “This is Dover's bill. I've marked several items. Returning them would lower the debt by more than thirty pounds. I haven't marked any jewelry.” The jewelry was a bitter matter for Lydgate himself, but he had argued sternly with himself until he overcame the feeling. He could not ask Rosamond to return any particular gift he had given her. Still, he told himself he was obliged to explain Dover's offer. Her own impulse might make the matter easy.

“There's no point in my looking, Tertius,” Rosamond said calmly. “You'll send back whatever you please.” She would not look at the paper. Flushing to the roots of his hair, Lydgate drew it back and let it drop onto his knee. Rosamond quietly left the room, leaving him helpless and bewildered. Was she not coming back? She seemed to feel no more connection with him than if they belonged to different species with opposing interests. He tossed his head and thrust his hands deep into his pockets with a kind of vengeance. Science remained; there were still worthy aims to pursue. He must pull harder, all the harder as his other sources of happiness disappeared.

But the door opened and Rosamond returned. She carried the leather case holding the amethysts and a tiny decorative basket containing other boxes. Setting them on the chair she had occupied, she said with an air of perfect propriety:
“This is every piece of jewelry you've given me. Return whichever you like, and whatever silver you choose. Naturally, you won't expect me to stay here tomorrow. I'll go to Papa's.”
Many women would have found Lydgate's look more terrible than anger. It held a despairing acceptance of the distance she was placing between them.
“And when will you come back?” he asked, bitterness sharpening his voice.

“In the evening, of course. Naturally I won't mention it to Mamma.” Rosamond was certain no woman could behave more blamelessly than she was behaving. She went to sit at her worktable. Lydgate thought for a minute or two, then spoke with something of his old feeling:
“Now we're bound to each other, Rosy, you shouldn't leave me alone at the first trouble we encounter.”
“Certainly not,” Rosamond said. “I'll do everything that is proper for me to do.”

“It isn't right to leave this to the servants, or make me explain it to them. I'll have to go out, and I don't know how early. I understand how you shrink from the humiliation of money troubles. But my dear Rosamond, where pride is concerned—and I feel it as keenly as you—surely it's better to manage things ourselves and let the servants see as little as possible. You're my wife. You can't avoid sharing my disgraces, if there are disgraces.”
For a moment Rosamond said nothing. Then she answered, “Very well. I'll stay at home.”
“I won't touch the jewelry, Rosy. Take it back. But I'll make a list of silver we can return, so it can be packed and sent off at once.”
“The servants will know about _that_,” Rosamond said with the faintest hint of sarcasm.
“Well, some unpleasant things must be accepted as necessary. Where's the ink?” Lydgate stood up and tossed the bill onto the larger table, where he intended to write.
Rosamond fetched the inkstand. She set it on the table and was turning away when Lydgate, standing beside her, put an arm around her and drew her close.
“Come, darling, let's make the best of it. I hope we won't have to be stingy and careful for very long. Give me a kiss.”

His natural warmth was not easily extinguished. It is part of a husband's manliness to feel keenly that an inexperienced girl has come into trouble by marrying him. Rosamond accepted his kiss and returned it faintly, and for the moment they recovered an appearance of harmony. But Lydgate could not help dreading the inevitable discussions ahead about spending and the need to change their way of life completely.

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LIX
paragraphs:
“People once said the Soul was human-shaped,
But smaller, finer than the body,
And wandered out for air whenever it pleased.
Look! Beside her cherub's face there floats
A pale-lipped, airy figure, whispering
Its urgings into the small shell of her ear.”

News often spreads as carelessly and effectively as the pollen bees carry away, unaware of how dusty they are, while buzzing after their own particular nectar. This elegant comparison concerns Fred Vincy. That evening at Lowick Parsonage, he heard the ladies eagerly discussing news their old servant had obtained from Tantripp: Mr. Casaubon's strange reference to Mr. Ladislaw in a codicil added to his will shortly before his death. Miss Winifred was astonished that her brother already knew. She declared Camden extraordinary at knowing things and never telling them. Mary Garth suggested the codicil had perhaps become mixed up with spiders' habits, which Miss Winifred refused to hear about. Mrs. Farebrother thought the news explained why they had seen Mr. Ladislaw at Lowick only once. Miss Noble made a series of small, compassionate mewing sounds.

Fred knew little about Ladislaw and the Casaubons and cared less. He never thought of the conversation again until, stopping at Rosamond's one day to deliver a message for his mother, he happened to see Ladislaw leaving. Since marriage had freed Rosamond from the unpleasantness of living with brothers, she and Fred had little to say to one another. They had still less now that he had taken what she considered the foolish, even blameworthy step of abandoning the Church for work such as Mr. Garth's. Fred therefore preferred to discuss news he thought neutral. “Speaking of that young Ladislaw,” he repeated what he had heard at Lowick Parsonage.

Like Mr. Farebrother, Lydgate knew far more than he told. Once he began considering the relationship between Will and Dorothea, his guesses went beyond the facts. He imagined a passionate attachment on both sides, which seemed far too serious for gossip. Remembering Will's irritability when Mrs. Casaubon had been mentioned made him still more cautious. Taken together, what he knew and what he guessed increased his friendliness and patience toward Ladislaw. They helped him understand the indecision that kept Will in Middlemarch after announcing he would leave. It showed how separate Lydgate's mind was from Rosamond's that he felt no impulse to discuss it with her. Indeed, he did not entirely trust her to remain discreet with Will. On that point he was right, though he could not have imagined how her thoughts would push her to speak.
When she repeated Fred's news, Lydgate said, “Rosy, don't let even the slightest hint of this slip to Ladislaw. He's likely to flare up as though you'd insulted him. Naturally, it's painful.”

Rosamond turned her head and patted her hair, looking perfectly calm and indifferent. But the next time Will visited while Lydgate was away, she teased him about not having gone to London as he had threatened.
“I know everything. A confidential little bird told me,” she said, tilting her head prettily over the work she held up between her busy fingers. “There's a powerful magnet nearby.”
“There certainly is. Nobody knows that better than you,” Will answered with light gallantry, though inwardly ready to be angry.

“It's the most delightful romance. Mr. Casaubon jealous, realizing there was no one Mrs. Casaubon would rather marry, and no one more eager to marry her than a certain gentleman. Then he makes a plan to ruin everything by taking away her property if she marries that gentleman. And then—and then—and then—oh, I'm sure the ending will be wonderfully romantic.”
“Good God, what are you talking about?” Will said. His face and ears flushed, and his features seemed altered, as if he had been violently shaken. “Stop joking. Tell me what you mean.”
“You really don't know?” Rosamond asked. Her playfulness vanished. She wanted nothing more than to tell him and see the effects.
“I don't!” he replied impatiently.
“You don't know Mr. Casaubon's will says Mrs. Casaubon loses all her property if she marries you?”
“How do you know it's true?” Will demanded eagerly.
“My brother Fred heard it from the Farebrothers.” Will sprang from his chair and reached for his hat.
“I expect she prefers you to the property,” Rosamond said, watching him from a distance.
“Please say no more,” Will answered in a low, hoarse voice unlike his usual light one. “It's a vile insult to her and to me.” Absently he sat down again, staring ahead without seeing anything.
“Now you're angry with _me_,” Rosamond said. “It's very unfair to blame _me_. You ought to thank me for telling you.”
“I do,” Will answered abruptly, with the divided awareness of someone replying to questions while dreaming.
“I shall expect news of the wedding,” Rosamond said playfully.
“Never! You'll never hear of that wedding!”
After blurting out those words, Will stood, offered Rosamond his hand with the same sleepwalking air, and left.

Once he was gone, Rosamond rose and crossed the room. She leaned against a small cabinet and looked wearily out of the window. Boredom oppressed her, along with that dissatisfaction which in women's minds so often turns into petty jealousy. It rests on no actual claim and grows from no deeper passion than the vague demands of self-interest, yet it can drive actions as well as words. “There really isn't anything worth caring much about,” poor Rosamond thought. She remembered the family at Quallingham, who did not write, and considered that Tertius might come home and bother her about expenses. She had already secretly disobeyed him by asking her father for assistance. His final, decisive answer had been, “I'm more likely to need help myself.”

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LX
paragraphs:
Fine phrases certainly deserve praise, and always have.
—_Justice Shallow_.

A few days later—it was already late August—an event caused some excitement in Middlemarch. Under the distinguished direction of Mr. Borthrop Trumbull, the public could, if it chose, purchase Edwin Larcher, Esq.'s furniture, books, and pictures, all of them—as anyone could see from the handbills—the finest of their kind. This was not a sale prompted by a downturn in trade. Quite the reverse: Mr. Larcher's great success in the transport business had enabled him to buy a mansion near Riverston, already lavishly furnished by a celebrated spa physician. Indeed, the dining room contained such large frames full of expensive painted flesh that Mrs. Larcher felt uneasy until she discovered, reassuringly, that the subjects came from Scripture. Hence the splendid opportunity for buyers advertised so clearly in Mr. Borthrop Trumbull's handbills. His knowledge of art history enabled him to announce that the hall furnishings, to be sold without a reserve price, included a carving by a contemporary of Gibbons.

In the Middlemarch of that period, a large auction was a kind of festival. A table held the finest cold food, as at a superior funeral. Ample opportunities to drink cheerful glasses encouraged equally cheerful and generous bids on unwanted objects. In the fine weather, Mr. Larcher's sale was particularly attractive because the house stood at the town's edge, with a garden and stables, on the pleasant exit called the London Road. This was also the road to the New Hospital and Mr. Bulstrode's secluded home, the Shrubs. In short, the auction was as good as a fair, attracting every class with leisure to spare. For some, who risked bids simply to push up prices, it was almost as good as betting on horses. On the second day, when the finest furniture was offered, “everybody” attended. Even Mr. Thesiger, St. Peter's rector, briefly came to try for the carved table and rubbed shoulders with Mr. Bambridge and Mr. Horrock. Middlemarch ladies formed a seated ring around the large dining table. Mr. Borthrop Trumbull stood elevated there with desk and hammer. Behind them were rows of mostly male faces, continually changing as people entered and left through the door or the large bow window opening onto the lawn.

That day's “everybody” did not include Mr. Bulstrode. His health could not stand crowds and drafts. Mrs. Bulstrode, however, particularly wanted a picture: a “Supper at Emmaus,” attributed in the catalogue to Guido. Just before the sale, Mr. Bulstrode called at the “Pioneer” office, since he was now one of the paper's proprietors. He asked Mr. Ladislaw, as a special favor, to put his remarkable knowledge of painting at Mrs. Bulstrode's service and assess the picture's value. “Provided,” the banker added with meticulous courtesy, “attending the sale won't disturb your preparations to leave, which I understand is imminent.”

Had Will cared about such things just then, that qualification might have sounded rather satirical. Weeks earlier he had agreed with the paper's owners that, since he intended to leave Middlemarch for good, he could hand over at any time to the assistant editor he had been training. But vague visions of ambition are weak against the comfort of familiar work or anything seductively pleasant. We all know how hard it is to carry out a resolution we secretly hope will become unnecessary. In that state, even the greatest skeptic privately leans toward miracles. We cannot imagine how our wish could come true, but wonderfully strange things have happened! Will did not admit this weakness to himself, yet he stayed. What would be the use of going to London at that season? The men from Rugby who might remember him were away. As for political writing, he preferred to remain with the “Pioneer” for a few weeks. At this particular moment, however, as Mr. Bulstrode spoke, Will's determination to leave had strengthened—and so had his equally firm determination not to leave before seeing Dorothea once more. He therefore replied that he had reasons to postpone his departure a little and would gladly attend the auction.

Will felt defiant. It stung him deeply to think that people looking at him probably knew something that amounted to accusing him of low designs which a property arrangement was intended to thwart. Like most people who proclaim their independence of conventional distinctions, he was ready to quarrel instantly with anyone who suggested a personal motive behind that position: anything in his ancestry, manner, or character that he had disguised as an opinion. Under such an irritation, he would go about for days looking challenging. Color shifted in his clear skin as though he were constantly on the alert, watching for something to pounce upon.

At the auction this expression was especially marked. Anyone who knew only his gently eccentric or brightly happy moods would have noticed the contrast. He welcomed the opportunity to appear publicly before the Middlemarch tribes of Toller, Hackbutt, and the rest. They despised him as an adventurer while remaining savagely ignorant of Dante; they sneered at his Polish blood when their own breed badly needed an infusion from outside. He stood prominently near the auctioneer, a forefinger in each side pocket and his head tilted back, with no wish to speak to anyone. Mr. Trumbull had nevertheless warmly welcomed him as a “conny-sewer,” while exercising his own great faculties to the fullest.

Surely, among all men whose work requires a display of eloquence, none is happier than a successful provincial auctioneer who keenly appreciates his own jokes and feels the breadth of his encyclopedic knowledge. Gloomy, sour-blooded people might dislike constantly praising everything from bootjacks to “Berghems.” But a kindly fluid ran in Mr. Borthrop Trumbull's veins. Admiration came naturally to him. He would have liked to auction the universe, certain his recommendation would raise its price.

For now, Mrs. Larcher's drawing-room furniture was sufficient. When Will Ladislaw arrived, a second fireplace fender, supposedly forgotten in its proper place in the sale, suddenly demanded the auctioneer's enthusiasm. He distributed that enthusiasm on the fair principle of praising most what most needed praise. This fender was polished steel, with extensive pointed openwork and a sharp edge.

“Now, ladies, I appeal to you,” he said. “Here's a fender scarcely any other auction would offer without a reserve. With steel of this quality and a design so distinctive, it is, I might say, the sort of object”—Mr. Trumbull lowered his voice to a slightly nasal tone, tracing its outlines with his left forefinger—“that may not suit everyday tastes. Let me tell you, before long this workmanship will be the only fashion. Half a crown, did you say? Thank you. Half a crown for this characterful fender. I have particular information that antiques are much sought after in high circles. Three shillings—three and sixpence. Hold it higher, Joseph! Ladies, observe the purity of the design. Personally, I've no doubt it was made in the last century. Four shillings, Mr. Mawmsey? Four shillings.”

“I wouldn't put it in _my_ drawing room,” Mrs. Mawmsey said loudly enough to warn her rash husband. “I'm astonished at Mrs. Larcher. Any poor child falling against it would split their head in two. That edge is a knife.”

“Absolutely true,” Mr. Trumbull answered at once. “And extraordinarily useful to have a fender that cuts, should a leather shoelace or a piece of string need cutting when no knife is available. Many a man has been left hanging for want of a knife to cut him down. Gentlemen, if you had the misfortune to hang yourselves, this fender could cut you down immediately—with astonishing speed. Four and sixpence—five—five and six. An ideal item for a spare bedroom with a four-poster and a guest a little out of his mind. Six shillings. Thank you, Mr. Clintup. Going for six shillings—going—gone!” His gaze, which had been scanning the room with supernatural sensitivity to every hint of a bid, dropped to the paper before him. His voice also fell into brisk indifference. “Mr. Clintup. Get a move on, Joseph.”

“Worth six shillings to have a fender you can always tell that joke about,” Mr. Clintup said to his neighbor, laughing softly and apologetically. Though an eminent nurseryman, he was shy, and feared the audience would think his bid foolish.

Joseph had meanwhile brought a tray of small objects. “Now, ladies,” Mr. Trumbull said, picking one up, “here's a most recherchy collection: little treasures for the drawing-room table. Trifles make the sum _of_ human things. Nothing matters more than trifles. Yes, Mr. Ladislaw, yes, presently. Pass the tray around, Joseph. Ladies, you must examine these bijoux. What I hold is an ingenious device—a practical rebus, one might call it. Here it appears to be an elegant heart-shaped box, portable, for the pocket. Then it becomes a splendid double flower, an ornament for the table. And now”—he let the flower fall alarmingly into strings of heart-shaped leaves—“a book of riddles! Five hundred at least, beautifully printed in red. Gentlemen, if I had less conscience, I wouldn't encourage high bids. I covet it myself. What better promotes innocent amusement, and even virtue, than a good riddle? It prevents foul language and draws a man into the company of refined women. This clever object alone should command a high price for the whole lot, even without the elegant domino box, card basket, and so forth. Kept in one's pocket, it could make a person welcome anywhere. Four shillings, sir? Four shillings for this remarkable riddle collection and the other items. Here's a sample: ‘How do you spell honey to make it catch ladybirds? Answer: money.’ Did you hear? Ladybirds—honey—money. An amusement that sharpens the mind. It has a sting, what we call satire: wit without indecency. Four and sixpence—five shillings.”

The bids continued with growing rivalry. Mr. Bowyer was bidding, which was intolerably irritating. He couldn't afford it and only wanted to stop other men making an impression. Even Mr. Horrock was swept along. Yet he committed himself to an opinion with so little alteration of his neutral expression that no one might have known the bid was his without Mr. Bambridge's friendly curses. The horse dealer wanted to know what Horrock would do with such damned stuff, fit only for haberdashers condemned to that perdition in which he so heartily believed most earthly creatures lived. Finally, the lot went for a guinea to Mr. Spilkins, a local young Slender, careless with his pocket money and conscious of his poor memory for riddles.
“Really, Trumbull, this is too much. You've put an old maid's rubbish into the auction,” Mr. Toller murmured, drawing close. “I want to see what the prints fetch, and I must leave soon.”

“_Im_mediately, Mr. Toller. It was only an act of kindness, one your noble heart would approve. Joseph, the prints, quickly! Lot 235. Now, gentlemen, those of you who are conny-sewers are in for a treat. An engraving of the Duke of Wellington, surrounded by his staff on the field of Waterloo. And despite recent events that have, so to speak, cast a cloud over our great Hero, I venture to say—a man in my profession mustn't be blown about by political winds—that a finer subject of the modern kind, belonging to our own time and age, could hardly be imagined by the human mind. Angels perhaps, but not men, gentlemen, not men.”
“Who painted it?” Mr. Powderell asked, much impressed.
“It's a proof made before the lettering, Mr. Powderell. The painter isn't known,” Trumbull replied, almost gasping over the final words. Then he pursed his lips and stared around.
“I'll give a pound!” Mr. Powderell declared with determined feeling, like a man prepared to step into the breach. Whether out of awe or pity, no one bid against him.

Next came the two Dutch prints Mr. Toller had wanted. Once he secured them, he left. Other prints and then paintings went to leading Middlemarch residents who had specifically come for them. The audience began circulating more freely: some left with their purchases settled, others arrived for the first time or returned from refreshments under the marquee on the lawn. Mr. Bambridge intended to buy that marquee and seemed to enjoy frequent inspections of its interior as a foretaste of ownership. On his latest return, he brought a new companion, unknown to Mr. Trumbull and everyone else. The stranger's appearance suggested he might be a relative of the horse dealer, also “fond of indulgence.” Large whiskers, an imposing swagger, and a swinging gait made him conspicuous. But his black suit, frayed at the edges, prompted the unfavorable conclusion that he could not afford as much indulgence as he wanted.
“Who's this you've picked up, Bam?” Mr. Horrock asked quietly.
“Ask him,” Mr. Bambridge replied. “Said he'd just come in off the road.”

Mr. Horrock studied the stranger. He leaned backward on his stick with one hand, worked a toothpick with the other, and looked around restlessly, apparently constrained by the silence circumstances demanded.

At last the “Supper at Emmaus” was produced, to Will's immense relief. He had become so bored that he had drawn back and rested a shoulder against the wall just behind the auctioneer. Now he stepped forward again. His eyes met the conspicuous stranger's, and he was rather surprised to find the man staring pointedly at him. But Mr. Trumbull immediately addressed Will.

“Yes, Mr. Ladislaw, yes. This interests you as a conny-sewer, I think. It's a real pleasure,” the auctioneer continued with growing fervor, “to show a company of ladies and gentlemen a picture like this. To anyone whose means matched his judgment, it would be worth any sum. A painting of the Italian school, by the famous _Guydo_, the world's greatest painter, foremost among the Old Masters. I suppose we call them that because they knew a thing or two beyond most of us, possessed secrets now lost to most of mankind. Gentlemen, I've seen plenty of Old Masters, and they're not all this good. Some are darker than you might wish, and the subjects aren't suitable for families. But here is a _Guydo_—the frame alone is worth pounds—that any lady could proudly hang on her wall. It would be suitable for what we call a refectory in a charitable institution, should any gentleman of the Corporation wish to display his munifi_cence_. Turn it a little, sir? Certainly. Joseph, turn it toward Mr. Ladislaw. You see, Mr. Ladislaw has been abroad and appreciates the quality of these things.”
For a moment everyone looked at Will. “Five pounds,” he said calmly. The auctioneer erupted in profound protest.

“Oh, Mr. Ladislaw! The frame alone is worth that. Ladies and gentlemen, think of the town's reputation! Suppose it were discovered afterward that a jewel of art had been here and nobody in Middlemarch recognized it. Five guineas—five pounds seven and six—five pounds ten. Still, ladies, still! A gem, and ‘Full many a gem,’ as the poet says, has fetched a mere trifle because the public knew no better, because it was offered where there was—I was going to say a low appreciation, but no! Six pounds—six guineas. A first-rate _Guydo_ going for six guineas! Ladies, it's an insult to religion. As Christians, gentlemen, we're all affected when such a subject sells for so little. Six pounds ten—seven—”

Bidding grew brisk. Remembering how much Mrs. Bulstrode wanted the picture, Will kept bidding and thought he might go as high as twelve pounds. But it was knocked down to him at ten guineas. He pushed through to the bow window and went outside. Hot and thirsty, he entered the marquee for water. No other visitors were there. He asked the woman attending it to bring him some fresh water, but she had scarcely left when the florid stranger who had stared at him came in. Will felt annoyed. It occurred to him that this might be one of those bloated political parasites who had once or twice claimed acquaintance because they had heard him speak on Reform, and who might hope to earn a shilling by bringing news. Seen that way, the man's appearance, already heating enough to look at on a summer day, became still more unpleasant. Half seated on a garden chair's arm, Will deliberately turned his eyes away. Such a hint meant little to our acquaintance Mr. Raffles, who never hesitated to force himself on an unwilling person's attention when it suited him. He moved a pace or two until he faced Will and spoke with full-mouthed haste. “Excuse me, Mr. Ladislaw. Was your mother's name Sarah Dunkirk?”
Will sprang up and stepped backward, frowning. “Yes, sir, it was,” he said fiercely. “What business is that of yours?”

Will's instinct was to answer the question directly and challenge whatever followed. To begin by asking what business it was of the other person's would have seemed evasive—as though he cared who knew about his origins!

Raffles did not share the eagerness for a clash suggested by Ladislaw's threatening stance. The slender young man, with his girl's complexion, looked like a wildcat ready to spring. In such circumstances, Mr. Raffles restrained his enjoyment of irritating people.

“No offense, my good sir, none at all! I simply remember your mother. Knew her as a girl. But it's your father you resemble, sir. I had the pleasure of seeing him too. Are your parents alive, Mr. Ladislaw?”
“No!” Will thundered, holding the same position.
“I'd be happy to do you a service, Mr. Ladislaw. By Jove, I would! Hope we'll meet again.”

Raffles lifted his hat as he spoke, then turned with a swing of his leg and walked away. Will watched briefly. The man did not return to the auction room, but seemed to be heading toward the road. For an instant Will thought he had been foolish not to let him continue. No, though: on the whole he preferred doing without information from that source.

Later that evening, however, Raffles caught up with him in the street. Either he had forgotten his earlier rough reception or intended to avenge it with forgiving familiarity. He greeted Will jovially, fell into step, and began by praising the town and surrounding country. Will suspected he had been drinking and was considering how to escape when Raffles said:

“I've traveled abroad myself, Mr. Ladislaw. Seen the world. Used to speak a bit of parley-voo. Boulogne was where I saw your father. You're extraordinarily like him, by Jove! Mouth, nose, eyes, hair brushed back off the forehead just the same, rather foreign-looking. John Bull doesn't go in much for that. But your father was very ill when I saw him. Lord, lord, you could see through his hands. You were a little fellow then. Did he recover?”
“He didn't,” Will answered curtly.

“Ah, well! I've often wondered what became of your mother. Ran away from her people when she was a young girl. Proud spirit, and pretty, by Jove! I knew why she ran away.” Raffles looked sideways at Will and winked slowly.
“You know nothing dishonorable about her, sir,” Will said, turning on him fiercely. Just then, however, Mr. Raffles was insensitive to differences of manner.

“Nothing at all!” He tossed his head decisively. “She was a little too honorable to like her people. That was it.” He winked slowly again. “Lord bless you, I knew everything about them. A bit in what you might call respectable theft. A receiving house for stolen goods, done in the grand style. None of your secret corners—first-class. A splendid shop, handsome profits, no mistake. But Lord, Sarah would never have known a thing. A dashing young lady, she was. Fine boarding school, fit to marry a lord. Only Archie Duncan flung it in her face out of spite because she wouldn't have him. So she ran away from the whole business. I traveled for them, sir, in a gentlemanly capacity, on a high salary. At first they didn't mind her running off. Religious people, sir, very religious, and she wanted the stage. The son was alive then, so the daughter didn't count for much. Well, here's the Blue Bull! What do you say, Mr. Ladislaw? Shall we go in for a glass?”
“No. I must wish you good evening,” said Will. He darted into a passage leading to Lowick Gate and almost ran to put himself beyond Raffles's reach.

He walked a long way out of town along the Lowick road, welcoming the starlit darkness as it came. He felt as though dirt had been thrown over him amid jeers. One thing supported the man's story: his mother had always refused to explain why she had left her family.

Well, even if the truth about that family were as ugly as possible, how did it make him, Will Ladislaw, any worse? His mother had faced hardship to break with them. But had Dorothea's friends known this story—had the Chettams known—they would have found a fine excuse for their suspicions, a welcome reason to consider him unfit to approach her. Let them suspect what they liked. They would discover their mistake. They would learn that the blood in his veins was as untainted by meanness as their own.

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LXI
paragraphs:
“Inconsistencies,” answered Imlac, “cannot both be right, but imputed
to man they may both be true.”—_Rasselas_.
That same night, Mr. Bulstrode came home from a business trip to Brassing. His good wife met him in the hall and led him into his private sitting room.
“Nicholas,” she said, her honest eyes fixed anxiously on his, “such an unpleasant man came here asking for you. He's left me quite upset.”
“What sort of man, my dear?” Bulstrode asked, already horribly certain of the answer.

“A red-faced man with big whiskers and the most insolent manners. He insisted he was an old friend and said you'd be sorry to miss him. He wanted to wait here, but I told him he could see you at the Bank tomorrow morning. So insolent! He stared at me and said his friend Nick had been lucky in his wives. I don't believe he would have left at all if Blucher hadn't broken his chain and come running round on the gravel. I was in the garden, you see, so I said, ‘You'd better leave. The dog's very fierce, and I can't hold him.’ Do you really know anything about a man like that?”

“I think I know who it is, my dear,” Bulstrode replied in his usual quiet voice. “An unfortunate, dissolute creature I helped too generously years ago. Still, I expect he won't trouble you again. He'll probably come to the Bank—begging, no doubt.”

They said nothing more about it until the following day, when Bulstrode had come back from town and was dressing for dinner. Unsure whether he was home, his wife looked into his dressing room. He had taken off his coat and cravat and stood with one arm resting on a chest of drawers, staring blankly at the floor. He gave a nervous start and looked up when she came in.
“Nicholas, you look terribly ill. Is something wrong?”
“My head is very painful,” said Bulstrode. He suffered so often from poor health that his wife was always willing to accept it as the reason for his low spirits.
“Sit down. Let me bathe it with vinegar.”

His body had no need of the vinegar, but her loving attention comforted his spirit. Though invariably polite, he generally accepted such care with the coolness of a husband receiving what was due to him. Today, however, as she bent over him, he said, “You're very good to me, Harriet.” Something in his voice was new to her. She could not have said what it was, but her concern flashed into the thought that he might be about to fall seriously ill.
“Has something upset you?” she asked. “Did that man come to the Bank?”
“Yes. It was just as I expected. He once had the chance to make something better of himself, but he's fallen into drunkenness and debauchery.”

“Has he gone away for good?” Mrs. Bulstrode asked anxiously. She stopped herself, for particular reasons, from adding, “It was very unpleasant to hear him claiming to be your friend.” Just then she did not want to suggest her customary awareness that her husband's early connections were not quite the equal of her own. She knew little about them. He had first worked in a bank, then gone into what he called business in the City and made a fortune before he was thirty-three. He had married a widow much older than himself, a Dissenter, and probably inferior in various other ways of the sort a second wife, judging impartially, can usually discover in a first. Beyond this she had scarcely cared to inquire. His stories sometimes offered glimpses of his early religious interests, his wish to become a preacher, and his involvement in missionary and charitable work. She believed him an excellent man. His piety seemed particularly distinguished in someone who was not a clergyman; his influence had made her own outlook more serious; and his worldly possessions had raised her position. Yet she also liked to think that winning Harriet Vincy's hand had benefited him in every respect. Her family's standing was beyond question by Middlemarch standards, which surely cast a better light on things than any London street or dissenting chapel yard. The old provincial outlook distrusted London. And though true religion could save souls anywhere, honest Mrs. Bulstrode felt sure that salvation within the established Church was more respectable. She was so eager for others to overlook her husband's former life as a London Dissenter that she liked to avoid the subject even with him. He knew this perfectly well. In some ways he was rather afraid of his candid wife, whose borrowed piety and inborn worldliness were equally sincere. She had nothing to be ashamed of, and he had married her from a real affection that still endured. His fears, however, were those of a man concerned to preserve his acknowledged superiority. To lose his wife's high opinion—or anyone else's, unless they plainly hated him as an enemy of religious truth—would feel like the beginning of death. When she asked—
“Has he gone away for good?”
“Oh, I trust he has,” he replied, trying to sound as calmly unconcerned as possible.

In reality, Bulstrode was nowhere near a state of peaceful trust. During their interview at the Bank, Raffles had made it clear that his appetite for torment was almost as strong as his other appetites. He freely admitted he had made a detour to Middlemarch simply to look around and see whether it might suit him as a place to live. He had, certainly, found more debts waiting than he had expected, but he had not spent the whole two hundred pounds. A mere twenty-five would be enough to send him on his way for now. His chief desire had been to see his friend Nick and the family, and learn everything about the good fortune of someone so dear to him. Later he might come back for a longer visit. This time he refused to be “escorted off the premises,” as he put it: he would not leave Middlemarch under Bulstrode's supervision. He meant to take the coach the next day—if he felt like it.

Bulstrode knew he was powerless. Threats and persuasion were equally useless. He could rely neither on a lasting fear nor on a promise. Instead, his heart held the cold conviction that unless Providence intervened by sending death, Raffles would soon be back in Middlemarch. That certainty terrified him.

He was not facing prosecution or destitution. The only danger was that certain facts from his past would be exposed to his neighbors' judgment and his wife's sorrowful understanding. Those facts would make him an object of contempt and disgrace the religion with which he had so carefully identified himself. Fear of judgment sharpens the memory. It throws an inescapable light over the long-neglected past we have been accustomed to recall only in vague phrases. Even without memory, our life's growth and decline form a continuous chain of dependence; but vivid memory compels a man to acknowledge a blameworthy past as his own. When remembrance stings like a reopened wound, that past is no dead history, no discarded preparation for the present, no repented error shaken free of one's life. It is a living, trembling part of oneself, sending back shudders, bitter tastes, and the prickling heat of deserved shame.

Bulstrode's past had now returned to this second kind of life; only its pleasures seemed to have lost their force. Day and night, except for short spells of sleep that merely wove memory and fear into a fantastic present, the scenes of his earlier life stood between him and everything else. They persisted like the reflections that face us when we look out of a lighted room: instead of grass and trees, we see the objects behind our backs. The sequence of inner and outward events appeared all at once. He might dwell on each in turn, but the others never loosened their grip on his awareness.

He saw himself again as the young bank clerk: pleasant-looking, as good with figures as he was fluent in speech, and fond of defining points of theology. Though young, he had been a leading member of a Calvinist dissenting congregation in Highbury, with powerful experiences of sin and forgiveness to describe. Once again he heard himself called upon as Brother Bulstrode at prayer meetings, speaking from religious platforms and preaching in private houses. He remembered considering the ministry as a possible calling and feeling drawn to missionary work. Those had been his happiest days. That was the point in his life at which he would now have chosen to wake and discover that everything since had been a dream. The circle in which Brother Bulstrode stood out was small, but its members were close to him, and that closeness deepened his satisfaction. His power extended over little ground, yet he felt its effect all the more intensely. He found it easy to believe that grace had worked exceptionally within him and that the signs marked him out as a special instrument of God.

Then came the turning point. An orphan educated at a charitable commercial school, he had felt himself promoted when Mr. Dunkirk, the wealthiest member of the congregation, invited him to his fine villa. Soon he was a familiar guest. The wife honored his piety; the husband recognized his ability. Dunkirk's fortune came from a flourishing trade in the City and the West End. This redirected Bulstrode's ambition. His future usefulness to God now seemed to lie in combining outstanding religious gifts with success in business.

In time there came what looked like a clear outward direction. A trusted junior partner died, leaving a vacancy the principal keenly felt. He could imagine no one better suited to fill it than his young friend Bulstrode, if Bulstrode would agree to become his confidential accountant. Bulstrode accepted. It was a pawnbroking business, magnificent in both its scale and its profits. Before long he discovered that one source of those magnificent profits was a willingness to accept any goods offered without asking searching questions about where they came from. But the firm had a West End branch, and nothing shabby or small about it suggested that one should feel ashamed.

He remembered his first recoil. It took place in private and was accompanied by arguments, some of which took the form of prayer. The business was established, with roots stretching far back. Surely opening a new gin palace was one thing and accepting an investment in an existing one another? Where, in human dealings, could anyone draw the boundary at which profits made from lost souls began? Wasn't this even God's method of saving His chosen? “You know,” the young Bulstrode had said, just as the older man was saying now, “you know how little my soul is attached to these things. I see them only as tools for cultivating your garden, reclaimed here and there from the wilderness.”

He had plenty of metaphors and precedents, and no shortage of special spiritual experiences. Eventually these made staying in his position seem a service required of him. The prospect of a fortune had already opened before him, and his misgivings remained private. Mr. Dunkirk had never expected misgivings at all: he had never imagined that trade had anything to do with the plan of salvation. Bulstrode did, in fact, lead two separate lives. His religious work could not conflict with his business once he had reasoned himself out of feeling any conflict.

Now, surrounded again in thought by that past, he offered the same defenses. Indeed, over the years he had kept spinning them into denser and more tangled webs that cushioned his moral sense. As age made his self-interest more eager while giving him less enjoyment, his soul had grown still more steeped in the conviction that he did everything for God's sake and cared nothing for himself. Yet if he could return to that distant time, with all the poverty of his youth, he would choose to be a missionary.

But the chain of causes into which he had fastened himself continued. Trouble came to the fine villa at Highbury. Years earlier, the only daughter had run away, defied her parents, and gone on the stage. Now the only son died, and shortly afterward Mr. Dunkirk died too. His wife, a simple, devout woman, was left with all the wealth both inside and outside that magnificent business, whose exact nature she had never understood. She had come to trust Bulstrode and to adore him innocently, as women often adore their priest or their minister appointed by men. It was natural that, after a while, they should think of marriage. But Mrs. Dunkirk felt troubled longings for her daughter, who had long been treated as lost to both God and her parents. They knew the daughter had married, but she had vanished completely. Having lost her boy, the mother pictured a grandson and wanted to reclaim her daughter in both senses of the word. If the daughter were found, some of the wealth—perhaps a large share—would go toward providing for several grandchildren. Before Mrs. Dunkirk would marry again, they must try to find her. Bulstrode agreed. But after advertisements and other inquiries failed, the mother believed her daughter could not be found and consented to marry without setting any property aside.
The daughter had been found. Only one man besides Bulstrode knew it, and he had been paid to keep quiet and go away.

That was the naked fact Bulstrode was now forced to confront, with the hard outline an action presents to an outsider. To him at the time, and even now in his burning memory, it had been divided into little steps. Each step had been justified as he took it by arguments that seemed to establish its righteousness. He believed remarkable acts of Providence had sanctioned his course up to then. They seemed to point toward his becoming the agent who would put a large fortune to its best use and rescue it from misuse. Death, and other striking arrangements such as a woman's trusting nature, had intervened. Bulstrode would have echoed Cromwell: “Do you call these mere events? May the Lord pity you!” The events were relatively small, but the essential condition was present: they favored his own purposes. He could easily decide what he owed others by asking what God intended for him. Would God's service benefit if a considerable part of this fortune went to a young woman and her husband devoted to frivolous pursuits, who might squander it on trivial things? Such people seemed outside the course of special providence. Bulstrode had never told himself in advance, “The daughter must not be found.” Nevertheless, when the moment came, he concealed her existence. Later, he comforted the mother with the thought that the unhappy young woman was probably dead.

There were times when he felt he had acted wrongly, but how could he turn back? He performed spiritual exercises, called himself nothing, held fast to redemption, and continued serving as God's instrument. Five years later, Death widened his path again by taking his wife. He gradually withdrew his capital, but he did not make the sacrifices necessary to close the business. It continued another thirteen years before finally collapsing. Meanwhile, Nicholas Bulstrode had used his hundred thousand pounds prudently and become a solidly important figure in the provinces: a banker, a member of the Church, a public benefactor. He was also a silent partner in businesses where he applied his skill to reducing the cost of raw materials, as with the dyes that rotted Mr. Vincy's silk. Now, after almost thirty undisturbed years of respectability, during which everything earlier had lain numb in his awareness, that past had risen and flooded his mind. It was as though some terrible new sense had broken into existence and overwhelmed his frail being.

Meanwhile, his conversation with Raffles had taught him something momentous. It became an active force in the struggle between his desires and his fears. Here, he thought, was a possible opening toward spiritual rescue, and perhaps material rescue too.

His need for spiritual rescue was real. Some crude hypocrites may consciously pretend to beliefs and feelings in order to deceive the world, but Bulstrode was not one of them. He was simply a man whose desires had proved stronger than his professed beliefs, and who had gradually explained satisfying those desires until it appeared entirely consistent with those beliefs. If that is hypocrisy, it is a process that occasionally occurs in all of us, whatever our faith. It can happen whether we believe in humanity's future perfection or in the latest predicted date for the world's end; whether we consider the earth a rotting nest that preserves a chosen remnant, ourselves included, or passionately believe in human solidarity.

Throughout his life, the service he could render religion had been the reason he gave himself for his actions, the motive he poured into his prayers. Who would make better use of money and position than he intended? Who could surpass him in loathing himself and exalting God's cause? For Bulstrode, however, God's cause was separate from his own upright conduct. It required him to distinguish God's enemies, to use them only as instruments, and, if possible, to keep money and its accompanying influence out of their hands. Profitable investments in businesses where the prince of this world exercised his most active cunning became holy when God's servant put their profits to a righteous use.

This unspoken reasoning belongs no more exclusively to evangelical religion than the use of grand phrases to cover petty motives belongs exclusively to Englishmen. Any general doctrine can eat away our morality unless it is checked by a deeply rooted habit of direct sympathy with individual human beings.

Still, someone who believes in something beyond his own greed must have a conscience, some standard to which he adjusts himself more or less. Bulstrode's standard had been his usefulness to God's cause. “I am sinful and nothing—a vessel to be made holy through use—but use me!” Into that mold he had forced his enormous need to be important and dominant. Now a moment had come when the mold seemed in danger of shattering and being thrown away altogether.

What if the actions he had accepted because they strengthened him as an instrument of divine glory became an excuse for mockery and a cloud upon that glory? If Providence decreed this, he would be driven out of the temple as a man who had brought impure offerings.

He had long poured out declarations of repentance. Today, however, repentance had a more bitter taste. A threatening Providence was pressing him toward a form of appeasement that involved more than doctrine. The divine court looked different to him now. Humbling himself was no longer enough; he must come with restitution in his hand. It was truly before his God that Bulstrode was preparing to attempt whatever restitution seemed possible. Great dread had taken hold of his sensitive body, and the scorching approach of shame created a new spiritual need. Day and night, as the returning, threatening past formed a conscience within him, he considered how to regain peace and trust, what sacrifice might hold back the rod. In these frightened moments he believed that if he voluntarily did something right, God would spare him the consequences of doing wrong. Religion can change only when the feelings that fill it change; and a religion of personal fear remains close to the level of primitive superstition.

He had watched Raffles actually leave on the Brassing coach, which brought temporary relief. It lifted the pressure of immediate fear but did not end his inward struggle or his need to secure protection. At last he reached a difficult decision and wrote to Will Ladislaw, asking him to come to the Shrubs at nine that evening for a private conversation. Will was not particularly surprised. He supposed the request concerned some new idea about the “Pioneer.” But when he was shown into Bulstrode's private room, the banker's painfully exhausted face struck him. He almost asked, “Are you ill?” Then, checking the abrupt question, he merely asked after Mrs. Bulstrode and whether she was pleased with the picture bought for her.

“Thank you. She's very pleased. She's out with our daughters this evening. I asked you here, Mr. Ladislaw, because I have something to tell you of a very private—indeed, I would say sacredly confidential—nature. I imagine nothing could have been further from your thoughts than the existence of important past connections linking your history with mine.”

Will felt something like an electric shock. He was already acutely sensitive about connections with the past, and his agitation had scarcely subsided. His forebodings were unpleasant. It felt like a dream changing shape: the action begun by that loud, bloated stranger was being continued by this sickly figure of respectability with his pale eyes. At that moment the banker's subdued voice and smooth, formal speech repelled him almost as much as the opposite manner he remembered. His color changed visibly as he answered—
“No. Nothing at all.”

“You see before you, Mr. Ladislaw, a deeply afflicted man. Nothing obliges me to make the disclosure for which I've asked you here tonight except the urgency of my conscience and the knowledge that I stand before One who sees differently from man. Under human law, you have no claim on me of any kind.”
Will felt more uneasy than curious. Bulstrode paused with his head resting on his hand, his eyes on the floor. Then he looked searchingly at Will and said—
“I am told your mother's name was Sarah Dunkirk and that she left her family to go on the stage. I'm also told your father was once severely wasted by illness. Can you confirm these things?”

“Yes. All of that is true,” Will said. He was struck by the timing of the question: surely such an inquiry should have preceded the banker's hints. But tonight Bulstrode had followed the order of his feelings. He had no doubt that the opportunity to make restitution had arrived, and an overwhelming urge drove him to expressions of repentance through which he hoped to avert punishment.
“Do you know anything more about your mother's family?” he went on.
“No. She didn't like talking about them. She was an extremely generous and honorable woman,” Will said, almost angrily.
“I don't mean to accuse her of anything. Did she never say anything at all about her mother?”
“I heard her say she believed her mother didn't know why she had run away. She used to say ‘poor mother’ in a pitying voice.”

“Her mother became my wife,” said Bulstrode. He paused before continuing. “You have a claim on me, Mr. Ladislaw. As I've said, it is not a legal claim, but my conscience acknowledges it. That marriage made me wealthy. This would probably not have happened—certainly not to the same degree—if your grandmother had been able to find her daughter. I understand that daughter is no longer alive?”

“No,” said Will. Suspicion and disgust rose in him so powerfully that, scarcely aware of what he was doing, he picked up his hat from the floor and stood. Everything in him wanted to reject this newly revealed connection.
“Please sit down, Mr. Ladislaw,” Bulstrode said anxiously. “Naturally the sudden discovery has startled you. But I beg you to be patient with someone already weighed down by inward suffering.”
Will sat again. He felt a little pity, half mixed with contempt, at the sight of an elderly man choosing to abase himself.

“Mr. Ladislaw, I want to make up for the loss your mother suffered. I know you have no fortune, and I wish to provide you with an adequate income from wealth that would probably already be yours if your grandmother had known for certain that your mother was alive and could have found her.”

Bulstrode stopped. He felt that his listener must see this as a striking example of conscientiousness, while God would see an act of repentance. He had no idea what was passing through Will's mind. Raffles's unmistakable hints still smarted there, and Will's natural quickness at putting things together was sharpened by the expectation of discoveries he would gladly have banished back into darkness. For several moments he gave no answer. At the end of his speech Bulstrode had looked down; now he raised his eyes inquiringly. Will met his gaze directly and said—
“I suppose you knew my mother was alive, and knew where she could be found.”

Bulstrode recoiled. His face and hands visibly trembled. He had been entirely unprepared for this response to his offer, or for being pressed into revealing more than he had decided was necessary. At that moment, however, he dared not lie. Suddenly the ground on which he had stood with some confidence felt uncertain.

“I won't deny that your guess is correct,” he answered unsteadily. “And I wish to make amends to you, as the only person still living who suffered a loss through me. I hope you understand my purpose, Mr. Ladislaw. It concerns claims higher than human ones and, as I've already said, is wholly independent of any legal obligation. I am prepared to reduce my own resources and my family's expectations by committing myself to pay you five hundred pounds a year for as long as I live, and to leave you a corresponding sum of capital at my death. Indeed, I would do more if some worthy undertaking of yours clearly required it.” Bulstrode had moved on to these details in the expectation that they would make a powerful impression on Ladislaw and absorb his other feelings into grateful acceptance.
But Will looked utterly stubborn, his lower lip thrust out and his fingers in his side pockets. The offer had not moved him at all. He said firmly—
“Before I answer your proposal, Mr. Bulstrode, I must ask you a question or two. Were you involved in the business that originally produced this fortune?”
“Raffles has told him,” Bulstrode thought. How could he refuse to answer when his own voluntary disclosure had prompted the question? He said, “Yes.”
“And was that business thoroughly dishonorable, or wasn't it? If its nature had become public, might the people involved have been classed with thieves and convicts?”
A cutting bitterness filled Will's voice. He wanted to put the question as starkly as possible.

Bulstrode flushed with anger he could not suppress. He had prepared himself for a scene of self-humiliation, but his fierce pride and habit of authority overcame repentance and even fear when the young man he intended to benefit turned on him like a judge.
“The business existed before my involvement, sir. Nor is it your place to conduct an inquiry of that sort.” His voice remained low, but his answer came with sharp defiance.

“Yes, it is,” Will said, springing up again, hat in hand. “It is very much my place to ask when I have to decide whether to deal with you and accept your money. My good name matters to me.
