It matters that there should be no stain on my birth or my connections. Now I find there is a stain I can do nothing about. My mother felt it and tried to keep as far from it as she could. I shall do the same. Keep your ill-gotten money. If I had a fortune of my own, I'd gladly give it to anyone who could prove that what you've told me is untrue. The one thing I can thank you for is keeping the money until now, when I'm able to refuse it. Whether a man is a gentleman ought to depend on the man himself. Good night, sir.”

Bulstrode was about to reply, but Will had left the room with determined speed. A moment later the front door closed behind him. His furious rebellion against this inherited stain, forced upon his knowledge, was too strong for him to consider just then whether he had treated Bulstrode too harshly. Perhaps he had shown an arrogant lack of mercy to a man of sixty trying to put things right after time had made the attempt futile.

No outside listener could have fully understood the force of Will's rejection or the bitterness of his language. Only he knew how immediately everything touching his sense of personal dignity affected his relationship with Dorothea and his feelings about Casaubon's treatment of him. Among the impulses that drove him to fling Bulstrode's offer back was the knowledge that he could never have told Dorothea he had accepted it.

After Will had gone, Bulstrode suffered a violent reaction and wept like a woman. Never before had a man of any higher standing than Raffles expressed open contempt for him. That contempt coursed through him like poison, leaving him unable to feel any consolation. Yet he had to stop even the relief of weeping. His wife and daughters soon returned from hearing a missionary to the East. They were full of regret that Papa had not heard for himself the interesting things they tried to repeat.
Perhaps, among all his hidden thoughts, the one that offered most comfort was that Will Ladislaw, at least, was unlikely to tell anyone what had happened that evening.

chapters.title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LXII
paragraphs:
He was a squyer of lowe degre,
That loved the king’s daughter of Hungrie.
—_Old Romance_.

Will Ladislaw now wanted only to see Dorothea again and then leave Middlemarch at once. The morning after his distressing encounter with Bulstrode, he wrote her a short letter. Various circumstances, he explained, had kept him in the neighborhood longer than expected. He asked permission to visit Lowick again at whatever hour she named on the earliest day possible. He was eager to leave, but unwilling to go before she had agreed to see him. He left the letter at the office with instructions for the messenger to take it to Lowick Manor and wait for a reply.

Will knew how awkward it was to ask for another farewell. Sir James Chettam had heard the previous one, and even the butler had been told it was final. Reappearing when one is not expected certainly tests a man's dignity. A first goodbye has pathos; returning for a second gives comedy its opportunity. People might even be sneering bitterly at Will's reasons for staying. Nevertheless, he felt better about taking the most direct route to seeing Dorothea than about arranging an apparently accidental meeting. He wanted her to understand that he earnestly sought it. When they had last parted, he had been unaware of facts that changed their relationship and separated them more absolutely than he had understood. He knew nothing about her private fortune. Having little practice in thinking about such matters, he assumed Casaubon's arrangements meant that if she married him, Will Ladislaw, she would be agreeing to become penniless. He could not wish that even in his most secret thoughts, even if she were willing to endure so harsh a change for his sake. There was also the fresh pain of the revelation about his mother's family. If that became known, it would give Dorothea's friends another reason to regard him as utterly beneath her. He had secretly hoped that after some years he might return with a sense that his personal worth at least equaled her wealth. Now that hope seemed one dream prolonging another. Surely this change justified asking to see her once more.

But Dorothea was away that morning and did not receive his note. Her uncle had written that he planned to return in a week. She had driven first to Freshitt with the news, intending to go on to the Grange and deliver some instructions he had entrusted to her. As he said, he thought “a little mental occupation of this sort good for a widow.”

Had Will heard some of that morning's conversation at Freshitt, he would have found all his suspicions confirmed about certain people's readiness to sneer at his continued presence. Although Sir James felt much reassured about Dorothea, he had been watching for news of Ladislaw's movements. Mr. Standish, necessarily taken into his confidence on this matter, had instructions to keep him informed. Ladislaw had remained in Middlemarch for nearly two months after declaring he would leave at once. This sharpened Sir James's suspicions, or at least justified his dislike of a “young fellow” whom he pictured as shallow and unstable. Such a man would probably show the recklessness natural to someone whose position was secured by neither family ties nor a strict profession. But Standish had just told him something which, while confirming these ideas about Will, also offered a way of eliminating any danger to Dorothea.

Unusual circumstances can make any of us act unlike ourselves. Even the most majestic person must sneeze under certain conditions, and our emotions can be affected in an equally undignified way. That morning, good Sir James was so unlike himself that he was anxiously irritable to speak to Dorothea on a subject he normally avoided as though it shamed them both. He could not speak through Celia: he did not want her to know the sort of gossip occupying his mind. Before Dorothea's arrival he had been trying to imagine how a shy man, with words that never came readily, could possibly introduce it. Her unexpected presence destroyed his remaining confidence in his ability to say anything unpleasant. Desperation, however, suggested a solution. He sent a groom across the park on an unsaddled horse with a penciled note to Mrs. Cadwallader. She already knew the gossip and would see no loss of dignity in repeating it whenever required.

They kept Dorothea there on the perfectly good excuse that Mr. Garth, whom she wanted to see, was expected at the hall within the hour. She was still talking to Caleb on the gravel when Sir James, watching for the Rector's wife, saw her approach and went to meet her with the necessary hints.
“Enough! I understand,” Mrs. Cadwallader said. “You can keep your innocence. I'm already black enough that another smudge won't show.”

“I don't mean that it matters very much,” said Sir James, uncomfortable at how much she understood. “Only Dorothea ought to know there are reasons she shouldn't receive him again. I really can't tell her myself. Coming from you, it will sound casual.”

Very casual it sounded. When Dorothea left Caleb and turned to meet them, it appeared that Mrs. Cadwallader had happened to cross the park quite by chance, simply for a motherly chat with Celia about the baby. So Mr. Brooke was coming home? How delightful! One hoped he had recovered completely from parliamentary fever and pioneering. Speaking of the “Pioneer,” someone had predicted it would soon resemble a dying dolphin, changing through every color because it had no idea how to save itself. Mr. Brooke's protégé, the brilliant young Ladislaw, had gone, or was going. Had Sir James heard?
They walked slowly along the gravel. Sir James turned aside to strike a shrub with his whip and said he had heard something of the kind.

“Entirely untrue!” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “Apparently he hasn't gone and isn't going. The ‘Pioneer’ keeps its color, while Mr. Orlando Ladislaw is creating a thoroughly blue scandal by endlessly warbling with the wife of your Mr. Lydgate. They tell me she's as pretty as can be. Nobody seems able to enter the house without finding the young gentleman stretched on the rug or singing at the piano. But people in manufacturing towns are always disreputable.”

“You began by telling us one report was false, Mrs. Cadwallader, and I believe this one is false as well,” Dorothea said with fierce indignation. “At least, I'm certain it distorts the truth. I will not listen to people speaking badly of Mr. Ladislaw. He's suffered quite enough injustice already.”

Once deeply moved, Dorothea cared little what anyone thought of her feelings. Even if she had stopped to consider, she would have thought it petty to let harmful remarks about Will pass unanswered merely from fear of being misunderstood herself. Her cheeks burned and her lip shook.

Sir James glanced at her and regretted his maneuver. Mrs. Cadwallader, however, was ready for anything. Turning her palms outward, she said, “Heaven grant it, my dear! I mean, may every ugly story about anyone turn out to be false. Still, it's a pity young Lydgate married one of these Middlemarch girls. Since he comes from somebody, he could have found a woman of good family, not too young, who would tolerate his profession. Clara Harfager, for instance: her friends don't know what to do with her, and she has some money. Then we might have had her among us. But there! It's no use being wise on other people's behalf. Where's Celia? Do let's go inside.”
“I'm going straight on to Tipton,” Dorothea said, rather proudly. “Goodbye.”
Sir James had nothing to say as he escorted her to the carriage. The scheme had already cost him a private humiliation; its result left him thoroughly dissatisfied.

Dorothea drove between hedges laden with berries and harvested cornfields, seeing and hearing nothing around her. Tears ran down her cheeks without her knowing. The world seemed to be growing ugly and hateful, with nowhere left for her trust. The voice she listened to within kept saying, “It isn't true—it isn't true!” Yet a memory that had always carried a vague uneasiness kept forcing itself upon her: the day she had found Will with Mrs. Lydgate and heard him singing to the piano.

“He said he would never do anything I disapproved of. I wish I could have told him I disapproved of that,” poor Dorothea thought. Her feelings swung strangely between anger with Will and a passionate desire to defend him. “They all try to make him seem bad to me. But I won't mind any pain, as long as he isn't to blame. I've always believed him good.” These were her last thoughts before she realized the carriage was passing under the arch of the Grange's lodge gate. She hurriedly pressed her handkerchief to her face and turned her mind to her errands. The coachman asked to take the horses out for half an hour because something was wrong with a shoe. Feeling that she could rest for a while, Dorothea removed her gloves and bonnet as she leaned against a statue in the entrance hall and spoke to the housekeeper. Finally she said—
“I'll have to stay a little while, Mrs. Kell. If you'll open the shutters, I'll go into the library and write down some instructions from my uncle's letter.”
“The shutters are already open, madam,” Mrs. Kell replied, following Dorothea, who had started along the hall as she spoke. “Mr. Ladislaw is in there looking for something.”
(While packing his belongings, Will had missed a portfolio of his own sketches. He had come to fetch it, unwilling to leave it behind.)

Dorothea's heart seemed to turn over as if struck, but she did not visibly falter. For the moment, simply knowing Will was there satisfied her completely, like finding something precious one had lost. At the door she told Mrs. Kell—
“Please go in ahead of me and tell him I'm here.”

Will had found the portfolio and set it on the table at the far end of the room. He was turning over the sketches and amusing himself with that memorable work of art whose connection with nature Dorothea had found too mysterious. He was still smiling at it, tapping the sketches into order and thinking that a letter from her might be waiting in Middlemarch, when Mrs. Kell spoke close beside him—
“Mrs. Casaubon is coming in, sir.”

Will turned sharply. A moment later Dorothea entered. They met as Mrs. Kell shut the door behind her. Each looked at the other, and something flooded their awareness that silenced speech. It was not embarrassment that kept them quiet. Both felt the nearness of parting, and a sorrowful farewell leaves no room for bashfulness.
Without thinking, she moved toward her uncle's chair by the writing table. Will pulled it out a little for her, then stepped a few paces away and stood facing her.

“Please sit,” Dorothea said, folding her hands in her lap. “I'm so glad you were here.” Will thought she looked just as she had when she first shook hands with him in Rome. The widow's cap attached to her bonnet had come off with it, and he could see she had been crying. Yet the anger mixed with her distress had vanished when she saw him. Face to face with Will, she had always felt trust and the happy freedom of mutual understanding. How could other people's words suddenly prevent that response? Let music that can possess our whole being and fill the air with joy sound again: what does it matter that we heard it criticized while it was absent?
“I sent a letter to Lowick Manor today asking if I might see you,” Will said, taking a seat opposite. “I'm leaving at once, and I couldn't go without speaking to you again.”
“I thought we'd said goodbye when you came to Lowick all those weeks ago. You thought you were leaving then,” Dorothea said, her voice shaking slightly.

“Yes. But there were things I didn't know then that I know now. They've changed how I feel about the future. When I saw you last, I still dreamed I might return one day. Now I don't think I ever shall.” He stopped.
“You wanted me to understand why?” Dorothea asked timidly.

“Yes,” Will said impulsively. He tossed his head back and looked away, irritation showing on his face. “Of course I do. I've been deeply insulted before you and everyone else. A mean insinuation has been made about my character. I want you to know that nothing could ever have made me stoop to—under no circumstances would I have allowed anyone to say I was pursuing money while pretending to pursue—something else. No further protection against me was needed. Wealth alone was protection enough.”

On the last word Will got up and walked away, scarcely knowing where he was going. He reached the nearest projecting window. It stood open, as it had at about this time the year before, when he and Dorothea had stood there talking. Her whole heart went out to him in sympathy with his indignation. All she wanted was to assure him that she had never misjudged him. Yet he seemed to have turned away as though she too belonged to the hostile world.

“It would be very unkind to think I'd ever believed anything mean of you,” she began. Then, eager to plead with him, she rose and moved in front of him, taking her old place in the window. “Do you think I ever lost faith in you?”

Seeing her there, Will started and stepped backward out of the window without meeting her eyes. Coming after his angry tone, the movement hurt Dorothea. She wanted to say that the situation was as hard on her as on him, and that she could do nothing. But the peculiar facts of their relationship, which neither could openly mention, kept her afraid of saying too much. Just then she did not believe that Will would have wanted to marry her under any circumstances, and she feared words that might suggest she did. Returning to his final phrase, she only said earnestly—
“I'm certain no one ever needed protection from you.”

Will gave no answer. Amid the storm of his changing feelings, her words seemed cruelly neutral. After his angry outburst he looked pale and miserable. He went to the table and strapped his portfolio while Dorothea watched from a distance. They were wasting their last moments in this wretched silence. What could he say when the thing that had seized hold of his mind was the passionate love he had forbidden himself to express? What could she say when she was allowed to offer him no help, when she had to keep money that ought to have been his, and when today he seemed unable to respond as he once had to her complete trust and affection?
At last, though, Will left the portfolio and came toward the window again.
“I have to go,” he said. His eyes had the peculiar look bitter feeling sometimes gives them, as if staring too closely at a light had scorched and exhausted them.
“What will you do with your life?” Dorothea asked shyly. “Are your plans still the same as when we said goodbye before?”
“Yes,” Will replied in a tone that dismissed the subject as uninteresting. “I'll work at the first thing that comes along. I suppose people get used to living without happiness or hope.”
“What a sad thing to say!” Dorothea was dangerously close to sobbing. Then she tried to smile. “We used to agree that we were alike in putting things too strongly.”

“I haven't put this too strongly,” said Will, leaning back against the corner of the wall. “There are experiences a man can have only once. Sooner or later he has to recognize that the best of his life is over. That's happened to me while I'm still very young, that's all. The thing I care about more than I can ever care about anything else is absolutely forbidden to me. I don't simply mean that I can't reach it. Even if I could, my own pride and honor would forbid it—everything for which I respect myself. Of course I'll go on living, like a man who has seen heaven in a trance.”

Will paused, certain Dorothea could not misunderstand. Indeed, he felt he was contradicting himself and violating his own standards by speaking so plainly. Still, telling a woman he would never court her could hardly be called courtship. It must be admitted that this was a rather ghostly form of it.

But Dorothea was rapidly reviewing the past with an entirely different picture before her. For an instant, the thought that she herself might be what Will cared for most sent a pulse through her. Then doubt returned. Their few shared experiences looked pale and small beside the thought of how much richer his relationship might have been with someone he saw constantly. Everything he had said could refer to that other relationship. Everything between Will and herself could be explained by what she had always understood as their simple friendship and the cruel obstacle her husband's damaging act had placed in its way. She stood silent, eyes dreamily lowered, while images crowded in and left her with the sickening certainty that Will meant Mrs. Lydgate. But why should it sicken her? He wanted her to know that here too his conduct would be beyond suspicion.

Her silence did not surprise him. As he watched her, his own mind was in turmoil. He felt, almost wildly, that something must prevent their parting: a miracle, since clearly no deliberate words of theirs could do it. Yet did she love him at all? He could not pretend he would prefer to believe her free of that pain. Beneath everything he had said lay a secret longing to be assured of her love. He could not deny it.
Neither knew how long they stood there. Dorothea was lifting her eyes and about to speak when the door opened and her footman announced—
“The horses are ready whenever you wish to leave, madam.”
“In a little while,” Dorothea replied. She turned to Will. “I have some notes to write for the housekeeper.”
“I must leave,” Will said when the door closed again, moving toward her. “The day after tomorrow I'm going away from Middlemarch.”
“You've done right in every way,” Dorothea said softly. A pressure at her heart made speech difficult.

She offered her hand. He took it briefly without a word. What she had said sounded cruelly cold to him, quite unlike her. Their eyes met: his held discontent, hers only sadness. He turned and tucked his portfolio beneath his arm.
“I've never thought unfairly of you. Please remember me,” Dorothea said, holding back a sob.
“Why say that?” Will asked irritably. “As though I weren't in danger of forgetting everything else.”

For a moment he was actually angry with her, and the anger drove him out without delay. To Dorothea it all passed in a single flash: his last words, his distant bow at the door, the realization that he was gone. She sank into the chair and sat motionless for a few moments as images and feelings rushed upon her. Joy came first, despite the threatening procession behind it. It was she whom Will loved and was giving up. There was no other, less permissible, more blameworthy love from which honor was driving him away. They were still separated, but Dorothea took a deep breath and felt her strength return: she could think about him without restraint. Just then their parting was easy to bear. The first awareness of loving and being loved left no room for grief. A hard, icy pressure seemed to have melted, giving her consciousness space to expand. Her past returned with a fuller meaning. The joy was no smaller—perhaps for that moment it was more complete—because their farewell was irrevocable. She had no reproach to imagine in anyone's eyes or words, no contemptuous surprise. He had acted in a way that defied reproach and made surprise respectful.

Anyone watching could have seen that a thought was strengthening her. When the creative mind works with happy ease, a small demand on its attention can be met completely, like a crack opening to admit sunlight. So Dorothea now found it easy to write her notes. Her final words to the housekeeper were cheerful. When she settled into the carriage, her eyes shone and her cheeks glowed beneath the gloomy bonnet. She pushed back its heavy mourning veils and looked ahead, wondering which road Will had taken. It was natural to her to feel proud that he was blameless. Through all her feelings ran the thought, “I was right to defend him.”

The coachman was accustomed to driving the grays briskly. Away from his desk, Casaubon had found no enjoyment in anything and had always been impatient to reach the end of a journey. Now Dorothea too was carried along swiftly. The drive was pleasant: overnight rain had settled the dust, and the blue sky seemed far away, beyond the region where great masses of cloud sailed. Beneath those vast heavens the earth looked a happy place. Dorothea wished she might catch up with Will and see him once again.

Around a bend, there he was, portfolio under his arm. A moment later she was passing him as he raised his hat. She felt a pang at sitting there in a kind of elevation while leaving him behind. She could not turn to look back. It was as though a crowd of indifferent objects had thrust them apart and forced them down separate paths, carrying them farther and farther from each other until looking back was useless. She could no more make a gesture that asked, “Must we part?” than stop the carriage and wait for him. Indeed, a whole world of reasons pressed against even allowing her thoughts to move toward a future that might undo today's decision.

“If only I'd known before! If only he knew! Then we could be perfectly happy thinking of each other, even though we're parted forever. And if only I could have given him the money and made things easier!” These longings returned most insistently. Yet despite her independent spirit, the world weighed heavily on her. Whenever she thought of Will needing help and struggling at a disadvantage, she also saw the supposed unsuitability of any closer connection between them, as everyone around her would judge it. She felt the full force of the motives driving his conduct. How could he imagine her defying the barrier her husband had placed between them? How could she ever tell herself she would defy it?

As the carriage shrank into the distance, Will's certainty held much more bitterness. In his sensitive state, the smallest thing could sting. Seeing Dorothea drive past while he trudged along like a poor devil seeking a place in a world that offered little he currently wanted made his conduct seem mere necessity. It robbed him of the support a deliberate resolve could give. After all, he had no assurance of her love. Could any man in such a position honestly claim to be simply glad that all the suffering was his alone?
Will passed that evening with the Lydgates. By the following evening he had left.

chapters.title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXIII
paragraphs: These little things are great to little man.—GOLDSMITH.
“Have you seen much lately of that scientific marvel of yours, Lydgate?” Mr. Toller asked Mr. Farebrother, seated on his right at one of his Christmas dinner parties.
“Very little, I'm sorry to say,” the Vicar replied. He was used to fending off Toller's teasing about his faith in the new medical star. “I live out of the way, and he's too busy.”
“Is he? How glad I am to hear it,” said Dr. Minchin, blending smooth politeness with surprise.

“He spends a great deal of time at the New Hospital,” Farebrother continued. He had reasons for pursuing the subject. “My neighbor Mrs. Casaubon tells me about it. She visits often. She says Lydgate works tirelessly and is making something excellent of Bulstrode's institution. He's getting a new ward ready in case cholera reaches us.”
“And getting his theories of treatment ready to test on the patients, I imagine,” Toller said.

“Come now, Toller, be fair,” said Farebrother. “You're much too clever not to recognize the value of a bold, fresh mind in medicine as in everything else. As for cholera, I suspect none of you is particularly certain what to do. If a man ventures a little too far down a new road, he generally does himself more harm than anyone else.”
“You and Wrench certainly ought to be grateful,” Dr. Minchin said, looking at Toller. “He's sent you the best of Peacock's patients.”
“Lydgate lives very extravagantly for a young man just starting out,” remarked Mr. Harry Toller, the brewer. “I suppose his family in the North supports him.”

“I hope they do,” said Mr. Chichely. “Otherwise he had no business marrying that lovely girl we were all so fond of. Damn it, you can't help resenting a fellow who carries off the prettiest girl in town.”
“And the best, by God!” Mr. Standish added.

“My friend Vincy wasn't at all pleased with the marriage, I know that,” Chichely said. “_He_ wouldn't contribute much. I couldn't say what the relatives on the other side may have put up.” His way of speaking made a point of seeming to withhold something.
“Oh, I shouldn't think Lydgate ever expected to earn his living from his practice,” Toller said with a touch of sarcasm. There the subject ended.

Farebrother had heard hints before that Lydgate's spending plainly exceeded the earnings of his practice. Still, he thought it quite possible that other resources or expectations had justified the outlay at his marriage and might prevent the disappointing practice from having serious consequences. One evening he made a special trip to Middlemarch to talk with Lydgate as in earlier days. He noticed a strained excitement quite unlike Lydgate's usual ease, whether sitting silent or breaking out with sudden energy when he had something to say. In his workroom, Lydgate talked continuously, weighing arguments for and against certain biological theories. Yet he had no definite result to explain or exhibit, none of the landmarks of patient, uninterrupted research on which he himself used to insist. “Every inquiry needs its systole and diastole,” he would say, and “A man's mind must keep expanding and contracting between the whole human horizon and the field of a microscope lens.” That evening, he seemed to range widely in conversation to prevent it from touching anything personal. Before long they joined Rosamond in the drawing room. Lydgate asked her to play for them, then sank silently into a chair, a strange brightness in his eyes. “Perhaps he's taken an opiate,” Farebrother thought. “Facial neuralgia, perhaps—or worries about his patients.”

It never occurred to him that Lydgate's marriage might be anything but happy. Like everyone else, he believed Rosamond sweet-tempered and compliant. He had always found her rather uninteresting, though: a little too much the perfect sample from a finishing school. His mother could not forgive her for seeming never to notice Henrietta Noble's presence. “Still, Lydgate fell in love with her,” the Vicar told himself, “so she must suit him.”

Farebrother knew Lydgate was proud. But he had so little of that pride himself, and perhaps cared too little about personal dignity apart from avoiding meanness or foolishness, that he could scarcely make enough allowance for Lydgate's reaction. The prospect of saying a word about his private affairs made Lydgate recoil as if from a burn. Soon after the dinner at Toller's, the Vicar learned something that made him look still more eagerly for a chance to suggest, indirectly, that if Lydgate ever wanted to discuss a difficulty, a friendly listener was ready.

The chance came at the Vincys' New Year's Day party. Farebrother could not resist their invitation: they insisted he must not desert old friends on his first New Year as a greater man, a Rector as well as a Vicar. It was a thoroughly friendly gathering. All the women of the Farebrother household attended, and all the Vincy children ate at the table. Fred had persuaded his mother that leaving out Mary Garth would insult the Farebrothers, since she was their particular friend. Mary came, and Fred was in high spirits, though his enjoyment was mixed. He rejoiced that his mother could see how highly the most important guests valued Mary, but jealousy sharply streaked that triumph whenever Farebrother sat beside her. Fred had felt much easier about his own accomplishments before he began to fear being “bowled out by Farebrother.” The danger still haunted him. Mrs. Vincy, in the full bloom of matronly beauty, looked at Mary's small figure, coarse wavy hair, and complexion without roses or lilies, and wondered. She tried unsuccessfully to imagine caring how Mary would look in wedding clothes, or taking satisfaction in grandchildren who would look like the Garths. Nevertheless, the party was merry, and Mary particularly lively. For Fred's sake she was glad his friends were warming to her. She was also quite willing to let them see how much others valued her—people whose judgment they had to respect.

Farebrother noticed that Lydgate looked bored and that Vincy spoke to his son-in-law as little as possible. Rosamond was perfectly composed and graceful. Only a closer scrutiny than the Vicar had felt prompted to give her would have detected the complete absence of the interest a loving wife inevitably shows in her husband's presence, even when etiquette keeps them apart. When Lydgate joined in the conversation, she looked no more toward him than a statue of Psyche sculpted to face elsewhere. When he returned after being called out for an hour or two, she appeared not to notice an event that eighteen months earlier would have transformed everything, like placing a numeral before a row of zeros. In fact, she was intensely aware of his voice and movements. Her pretty, good-natured air of indifference was a deliberate denial. Through it she satisfied her inward resistance to him while remaining perfectly proper. After Lydgate was called away during dessert, the women went to the drawing room. Rosamond happened to stand near Mrs. Farebrother, who said, “You must do without a great deal of your husband's company, Mrs. Lydgate.”
“Yes, a doctor's life is very demanding, particularly when he's as devoted to his work as Mr. Lydgate.” Having delivered this correct little speech, Rosamond moved away with ease.

“She's dreadfully lonely when there's no company,” said Mrs. Vincy, seated beside the old lady. “I certainly thought so when she was ill and I stayed with her. Ours is a cheerful house, Mrs. Farebrother. I'm cheerful by nature, and Mr. Vincy always likes something going on. That's what Rosamond grew up with. It's very different having a husband out at all hours, never knowing when he'll come home, and a reserved, proud sort of man, _I_ think.” Even indiscreet Mrs. Vincy lowered her voice a little for this aside. “But Rosamond has always had an angel's temper. Her brothers often displeased her, yet she was never one to show it. From babyhood she was as good as could be, and such a complexion! But thank God, all my children are good-tempered.”

Anyone watching Mrs. Vincy toss back her broad cap ribbons and smile toward her three younger daughters, aged seven to eleven, could readily believe her. But that smiling glance had to include Mary Garth. The girls had cornered Mary and made her tell them stories. She was just finishing the delightful tale of Rumpelstiltskin, which she knew by heart because Letty never tired of educating her ignorant elders from a favorite red book. Louisa, her mother's darling, ran over with wide eyes and solemn excitement. “Oh, Mamma! The little man stamped so hard he couldn't get his leg out of the floor!”

“Bless you, my little angel!” her mother said. “You can tell me all about it tomorrow. Go back and listen.” Watching Louisa return to that attractive corner, she decided that if Fred wanted Mary invited again, she would not object. The children liked her so much.

Soon the corner grew livelier still. Farebrother came in, sat behind Louisa, and lifted her onto his lap. All the girls insisted he must hear Rumpelstiltskin and Mary must tell it again. He insisted too. Without any fuss, Mary began again in her precise manner, using exactly the same words. Fred had also settled nearby. His pride in Mary's success would have been complete had Farebrother not watched her with obvious admiration while acting out an intense interest in the tale for the children's pleasure.
“You won't want to hear about my one-eyed giant anymore, Loo,” Fred said when she finished.
“Yes, I will. Tell us about him now,” Louisa replied.
“Oh, of course! I've been completely replaced. Ask Mr. Farebrother.”

“Yes,” Mary added, “ask him about the ants whose beautiful house was knocked down by a giant called Tom. He thought they didn't mind because he couldn't hear them crying or see them using their handkerchiefs.”
“Please?” Louisa asked, looking up at the Vicar.
“No, no. I'm a serious old parson. Whenever I reach into my bag for a story, out comes a sermon. Shall I preach you one?” He put on his spectacles for short-sightedness and pursed his lips.
“Yes,” Louisa said uncertainly.
“Now, let me think. Against cakes: how wicked cakes are, particularly sweet ones with raisins in them.”
Louisa took this rather seriously. She climbed off the Vicar's knee and went to Fred.

“Ah, I see New Year's Day isn't the time for preaching,” Farebrother said, getting up and moving away. He had lately realized that Fred was jealous of him. He had also realized that his own preference for Mary over every other woman was not fading.
“Miss Garth is a delightful young woman,” said Mrs. Farebrother, who had been watching her son.
“Yes,” Mrs. Vincy answered, obliged to reply when the old lady turned toward her expectantly. “It's a pity she isn't prettier.”

“I can't agree,” Mrs. Farebrother said firmly. “I like her face. We mustn't always demand beauty when a good God has chosen to make an excellent young woman without it. Good manners come first with me, and Miss Garth would know how to behave in any position.”

Her tone was slightly sharp because she was imagining Mary as her daughter-in-law. Mary's situation with Fred had the disadvantage that it could not appropriately be made public. The three ladies at Lowick Parsonage therefore still hoped Camden would choose Miss Garth.

More visitors arrived. The drawing room was given over to games and music, while whist tables were set up in the quiet room across the hall. Farebrother played a rubber to please his mother. She considered her occasional game a protest against slander and newfangled opinions, which gave dignity even to playing the wrong suit. Afterward he asked Chichely to take his place and left. As he crossed the hall, Lydgate had just arrived and was removing his overcoat.

“You're just the man I was looking for,” the Vicar said. Instead of going into the drawing room, they walked along the hall and stopped by the fireplace, where the frosty air helped the banked fire glow. Smiling at Lydgate, he continued, “You see how easily I can leave the whist table now that I don't play for money. Mrs. Casaubon says I owe that to you.”
“How so?” Lydgate asked coldly.

“Ah, you didn't want me to find out. I call that an ungenerous sort of secrecy. You should allow a man the pleasure of knowing you've helped him. I've never understood why some people dislike being obliged to others. On my word, I'd rather be obliged to everyone for treating me well.”

“I don't know what you're referring to,” Lydgate said, “unless it's that I once mentioned you to Mrs. Casaubon. But I didn't expect her to break her promise not to tell you.” He leaned against the corner of the mantel, his face showing no pleasure.

“Brooke let it slip the other day. He paid me the compliment of saying how glad he was I'd got the living, although you'd upset his plans. Apparently you praised me as another Ken or Tillotson and so forth, until Mrs. Casaubon wouldn't consider anyone else.”
“Brooke is such a loose-tongued fool,” Lydgate said contemptuously.

“Well, I was glad of his loose tongue on that occasion. My dear fellow, I don't see why you should mind my knowing you wanted to help me. And you certainly have. It puts quite a check on self-satisfaction to discover how much of one's good behavior depends on having enough money. A man won't be tempted to say the Lord's Prayer backward to please the devil if he has no need of the devil's services. I no longer have to wait on the favors of chance.”
“I don't see how anyone makes money without chance,” said Lydgate. “If he earns it through a profession, chance is almost certain to be responsible.”
This was so unlike Lydgate's former way of speaking that Farebrother explained it to himself as the perversity that often grows out of a troubled man's dark mood. He replied with cheerful agreement—
“Yes, the world's ways demand an enormous amount of patience. But waiting patiently is easier when a man has friends who love him and want nothing more than to help him through, as far as they can.”
“Oh, certainly,” Lydgate said carelessly, shifting his position and consulting his watch. “People make far more of their difficulties than they need to.”

He understood perfectly that Farebrother was offering to help him, and he could not bear it. Such strange impulses govern us: he had long enjoyed the knowledge that he had privately done the Vicar a service, yet the suggestion that the Vicar now saw his need for a service in return drove him into impenetrable silence. Besides, what must follow such an offer? He would have to “explain his circumstances,” hint that he needed specific things. At that moment, killing himself seemed easier.

Farebrother was too perceptive to miss the meaning of the reply. There was also something massive in Lydgate's manner and voice, matching his build, which seemed to rule out persuasion once he had rejected an approach.
“What time do you make it?” the Vicar asked, swallowing his hurt.
“Past eleven,” Lydgate replied. They went into the drawing room.

chapters.title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXIV
paragraphs: 1_st Gent_. Where lies the power, there let the blame lie too.

2_d Gent_. Nay, power is relative; you cannot fright
The coming pest with border fortresses,
Or catch your carp with subtle argument.
All force is twain in one: cause is not cause
Unless effect be there; and action’s self
Must needs contain a passive. So command
Exists but with obedience.

Even if Lydgate had wanted to speak freely about his affairs, he knew Farebrother could scarcely have supplied the help he needed at once. The year's bills were arriving from tradesmen. Dover's claim on his furniture hung over him. His only dependable income was the slow trickle of payments from patients he must take care not to offend: the generous fees from Freshitt Hall and Lowick Manor had been swallowed up readily enough. Nothing short of a thousand pounds would clear his immediate difficulties and leave a little over to give him, in the hopeful phrase people favor in such situations, “time to look about him.”

Merry Christmas and the happy New Year naturally brought the moment when fellow citizens expected payment for the goods and services they had smilingly supplied. These sordid cares now pressed so tightly on Lydgate's mind that he could scarcely think continuously about anything else, however familiar or compelling. He was not bad-tempered by nature. His active intellect, warmhearted kindness, and strong constitution would ordinarily have kept him above the petty, uncontrolled sensitivities that produce bad temper. But he was suffering from the worst kind of irritation. Beneath each annoyance lay another awareness: that he was wasting his energy on a degrading preoccupation, the opposite of everything he had once intended. “_This_ is what occupies me, and _that_ is what might have occupied me,” ran the bitter, unceasing murmur within. Every difficulty therefore pricked his impatience twice.

Some gentlemen have achieved remarkable literary reputations by expressing general dissatisfaction with a universe they consider a trap of dullness into which their great souls fell by mistake. But the sense of an enormous self in an insignificant world may offer consolations. Lydgate's dissatisfaction was harder to bear. He felt that a grand life of thought and useful action lay all around him, while his own life shrank into the miserable solitude of selfish fears and commonplace anxieties about events that might relieve them. His troubles may seem pitifully sordid, beneath the notice of elevated people who understand debt only on a magnificent scale. Sordid they certainly were. For the majority, who are not elevated, the only escape from such sordidness is freedom from craving money, with all its low hopes and temptations: waiting for someone to die, hinting at requests, wanting like a horse dealer to pass off bad work as good, seeking a post that ought to belong to someone else, and often being driven to long for a stroke of Luck in the shape of a widespread disaster.

Lydgate's horror at putting his neck under this degrading yoke had plunged him into the bitter mood that kept widening the distance between him and Rosamond. Since first telling her about the bill of sale, he had repeatedly tried to win her sympathy for ways of reducing their expenses. As Christmas approached threateningly, his suggestions became more definite. “The two of us can manage with one servant and live on very little,” he said. “And I can do with one horse.” As we have seen, he was beginning to think more clearly about living costs. Whatever pride he took in such outward appearances was slight compared with the pride that recoiled from being exposed as a debtor or asking other men for money.

“Of course you can dismiss the other two servants if you wish,” Rosamond said. “But I should have thought living poorly would damage your standing considerably. You must expect your practice to suffer.”

“My dear Rosamond, we don't have a choice. We started too expensively. Peacock lived in a much smaller house, you know. It's my fault. I should have known better. I deserve a beating, if anyone had the right to give me one, for forcing you to live with less than you're used to. But I suppose we married because we loved each other. That may help us get through until things improve. Come, darling, put your work down and come here.”

At that moment his feelings about her were cold and gloomy. Yet he dreaded a future without affection and was determined to resist the growing separation between them. Rosamond did as he asked, and he drew her onto his knee, though inwardly she remained utterly distant. The poor woman saw only that the world had not arranged itself to please her, and Lydgate was part of that world. He held her waist with one hand and gently laid the other over both of hers. This rather abrupt man could be very tender toward women, as though always conscious of their fragile bodies and the delicate balance of their physical and mental health. He began again, trying to persuade her.

“Now that I'm looking into things, Rosy, I'm astonished how much money disappears into the housekeeping. I suppose the servants are careless, and we've entertained a great many people. But plenty of people in our position must manage on much less. I suppose they use simpler things and keep an eye on leftovers. Money doesn't seem to go far in these matters. Wrench keeps everything as plain as possible, and he has an enormous practice.”
“If you're thinking of living like the Wrenches!” Rosamond said, turning her neck slightly. “I've heard you say how much you dislike their way of life.”
“Yes, their taste is dreadful in everything. They make saving money look ugly. We don't have to do that. I only meant that they avoid expense despite his excellent practice.”

“Why shouldn't your practice be good, Tertius? Mr. Peacock's was. You ought to take more care not to offend people and supply medicines as the others do. You certainly started well and secured several good households. Being eccentric can't pay. You should consider what people generally like.” Rosamond spoke with a small, definite note of correction.

Lydgate felt his anger rise. He was willing to indulge feminine weakness, but not feminine authority. A water sprite's shallow soul may seem charming until she starts giving lessons. He controlled himself, however, and said only, with a touch of commanding firmness—

“How I conduct my practice is for me to decide, Rosy. That isn't what we're discussing. You need only understand that our income will probably be very small for a long time—barely four hundred pounds, perhaps less. We must try to arrange our lives accordingly.”
Rosamond looked straight ahead in silence for a moment, then said, “My uncle Bulstrode ought to pay you a salary for the time you spend at the Hospital. It isn't right for you to work for nothing.”

“Everyone understood from the start that I would work without payment. That needn't come into this discussion either. I've told you the only likely prospect,” Lydgate said impatiently. Then he checked himself and continued more quietly—

“I think there's one way of freeing ourselves from a good part of the immediate difficulty. I hear young Ned Plymdale is marrying Sophy Toller. They're wealthy, and good houses don't often become available in Middlemarch. I'm sure they'd be glad to take this one with most of our furniture, and pay a handsome sum for the lease. I could ask Trumbull to approach Plymdale.”

Rosamond got off his knee and walked slowly to the far end of the room. When she turned back toward him, he could see tears in her eyes. She bit her lower lip and clasped her hands to stop herself from crying. Lydgate felt miserable, shaken by anger but certain it would be unmanly to let it out just then.
“I'm so sorry, Rosamond. I know how painful this is.”
“I thought that after I'd endured sending the silver back and having that man make a list of the furniture—surely _that_ should have been enough.”

“I explained then, darling. That was only security. Behind the security is a debt, and we have to pay it within the next few months or the furniture will be sold. If young Plymdale takes the house and most of the furniture, we can pay that debt and some others, and escape a place we can't afford. We could rent a smaller house. Trumbull has a perfectly decent one for thirty pounds a year, I know, while this costs ninety.” Lydgate delivered this in the short, hammering manner people use to pin a vague mind to unavoidable facts. Tears silently ran down Rosamond's cheeks. She merely pressed her handkerchief against them and stood staring at the large vase on the mantel. She had never felt such intense bitterness. At last she said slowly, emphasizing each word with care—
“I could never have believed you'd want to behave like this.”

“Want to?” Lydgate burst out. He rose, thrust his hands into his pockets, and strode away from the hearth. “It isn't about what I want. Of course I don't want it. It's the only thing I can do.” He wheeled around to face her.
“I should have thought there were plenty of other ways,” Rosamond replied. “Let's sell everything and leave Middlemarch altogether.”
“And do what? What good would it do to leave my work here for somewhere I have none? We'd be just as penniless anywhere else,” Lydgate said, angrier still.

“If that's the position we're to be in, Tertius, it will be entirely your own fault,” Rosamond said, turning to him with complete conviction. “You refuse to treat your family as you should. You offended Captain Lydgate. Sir Godwin was very kind to me at Quallingham. I'm sure that if you showed him proper respect and explained your situation, he'd do anything for you. But you prefer handing our house and furniture over to Mr. Ned Plymdale.”

Something fierce entered Lydgate's eyes. He answered with renewed violence, “Very well, if you insist, I do prefer it. I admit I'd rather do that than make a fool of myself begging where it will do no good. Understand, then: it is what I _want to do_.”

His tone in that last sentence was like the grip of his strong hand on Rosamond's delicate arm. Yet his will was no stronger than hers. She immediately left the room without speaking, intensely determined to prevent him from doing what he wanted.

He went out of the house. As his blood cooled, he realized that the conversation had chiefly left him dreading future discussions with his wife that might drive him into angry speech again. A crack seemed to have opened in delicate crystal, and he feared any movement that might break it beyond repair. Unless they could continue loving each other, his marriage would become a bitter joke. He had long ago accepted what he saw as her passive failings: her lack of sensitivity, shown in her disregard for both his particular wishes and his larger purposes. He had endured the first great disappointment. He must give up the tender devotion and obedient adoration of an ideal wife and resume life with lower expectations, like a man who has lost a limb. But his real wife still had both a claim upon him and a hold on his heart, and he desperately wanted that hold to remain strong. In marriage, the certainty “She will never love me much” is easier to bear than the fear “I shall stop loving her.” After his outburst, therefore, all his inward effort went into excusing her and blaming the hard circumstances for which he was partly responsible. That evening he tried through affection to heal the morning's wound. Rosamond was not naturally sulky or repellent. Indeed, she welcomed signs that her husband loved her and could be controlled. But this was quite different from loving _him_. Lydgate would have preferred not to return soon to the plan of giving up the house. He meant to carry it out with as little further discussion as possible. Yet Rosamond herself raised it over breakfast, asking gently—
“Have you spoken to Trumbull?”

“Not yet,” Lydgate said, “but I'll stop in as I pass this morning. We mustn't waste time.” He took the question as a sign that her inward resistance had ended, and kissed her head tenderly as he rose to leave.

As soon as visiting hours allowed, Rosamond went to Mrs. Plymdale, Ned's mother, and introduced the coming wedding with graceful congratulations. From a mother's perspective, Mrs. Plymdale thought Rosamond might now be seeing glimpses of her past foolishness. Since every advantage presently lay with her son, she was too kind a woman not to behave graciously.

“Yes, I must say Ned is wonderfully happy. And Sophy Toller is everything I could wish for in a daughter-in-law. Naturally her father can provide handsomely for her. With a brewery like his, that's only to be expected. The family connection is all we could desire too. But that's not what matters to me. She's such a nice girl, without airs or pretensions, though she's equal to the finest. I don't mean the titled aristocracy. I see little good in people reaching outside their own sphere. Sophy is as good as anyone in town, and she's content with that.”
“I've always found her very pleasant,” Rosamond said.

“I consider it a reward for Ned, who has never held his head too high, that he's made the very best connection,” Mrs. Plymdale continued. The warmth of her conviction that this was the correct view softened her natural sharpness. “The Tollers are so particular, they might have objected to our having friends they don't share. Everyone knows your aunt Bulstrode and I have been close since we were girls, and Mr. Plymdale has always supported Mr. Bulstrode. I prefer serious religious opinions myself. But the Tollers have welcomed Ned regardless.”
“I'm sure he's a very deserving young man with excellent principles,” Rosamond replied, neatly returning a little condescension for Mrs. Plymdale's wholesome corrections.

“Oh, he hasn't an army captain's style, or that way of carrying himself as though everyone else were beneath him, or those showy gifts for conversation, singing, and intellectual display. I'm thankful he hasn't. Such things prepare a man poorly for both this life and the next.”
“Oh, certainly. Appearances have very little to do with happiness,” said Rosamond. “I think they have every prospect of being happy together. What house will they have?”

“Well, they'll have to take what they can find. They've looked at the house in St. Peter's Place next door to Mr. Hackbutt. It belongs to him, and he's having it put in good repair. I doubt they'll hear of anything better. In fact, I think Ned will settle it today.”
“It must be a nice house. I like St. Peter's Place.”

“It's close to the church, and a respectable address. But the windows are narrow and the whole place is full of stairs and changes of level. You don't happen to know of another house becoming available?” Mrs. Plymdale fixed her round black eyes on Rosamond, animated by the sudden thought.
“Oh, no. I hear so little about such things.”

When Rosamond set out, she had not anticipated this question or her answer. She had only meant to gather information that would help her avoid losing her own house under circumstances she thoroughly disliked. She reflected no more on the lie she had just told than on the untruth of saying appearances had little to do with happiness. Her purpose, she was certain, was wholly justified. Lydgate's intention was the inexcusable one. She had a plan which, once completed, would prove how mistaken he would have been to lower himself from his present position.

On her way home she passed Borthrop Trumbull's office, intending to call. For the first time in her life, she was contemplating something in the nature of business, but she felt equal to it. The prospect of being forced to do something she intensely disliked turned her quiet persistence into active ingenuity. Here, mere disobedience and serene obstinacy would not suffice. She must act on her judgment, and she assured herself that her judgment was correct: “Indeed, if it weren't, I wouldn't want to act on it.”

Trumbull was in his back office and received her with his finest manners. Her charms appealed strongly to him, but kindness also stirred him. He knew Lydgate was in difficulties, and this exceptionally pretty woman, this young lady of the greatest personal attractions, would probably feel the pinch of trouble and find herself caught in circumstances beyond her control. He begged her to honor him by sitting down. Standing before her, he adjusted himself and his clothes with eager concern that was chiefly benevolent. Rosamond first asked whether her husband had called that morning about disposing of their house.

“Yes, ma'am, yes, he has. Indeed he has,” the kindly auctioneer said, trying to make the repetition soothing. “I intended to carry out his instructions this afternoon, if possible. He asked me not to delay.”
“I've come to ask you to take no further steps, Mr. Trumbull. And please don't mention anything that's been said about it. Will you do that for me?”

“Certainly, Mrs. Lydgate, certainly. I regard a confidence as sacred, whether in business or anything else. Then I should consider my instructions withdrawn?” He straightened the long ends of his blue cravat with both hands and looked at her respectfully.

“Yes, please. I've learned that Mr. Ned Plymdale has taken the house in St. Peter's Place next to Mr. Hackbutt. Mr. Lydgate would be annoyed to have his instructions carried out to no purpose. Besides, other circumstances have made the proposal unnecessary.”

“Very good, Mrs. Lydgate, very good. Whenever you need my services, I'm at your disposal,” Trumbull said, pleased to imagine that new resources had become available. “Please rely on me. The matter will go no further.”

That evening Lydgate found some comfort in Rosamond's being livelier than she had recently been. She even seemed interested in pleasing him without being asked. “If she's happy and I can struggle through, what does any of it matter?” he thought. “It's only a narrow swamp on a long journey. If I can clear my mind again, I'll manage.”

His improved spirits led him to search for an account of experiments he had long meant to consult. He had neglected it through the creeping loss of faith in himself that follows petty anxieties. Some of his old pleasure in absorption returned as he pursued a question with broad implications. Rosamond played quiet music, as helpful to his thinking as an oar's splash on an evening lake. It had grown late. He pushed the books aside and sat looking at the fire, hands clasped behind his head, forgetting everything except how to devise a new experiment to test his ideas. Rosamond had left the piano and was watching him from her chair when she said—
“Mr. Ned Plymdale has already taken a house.”
Startled and jarred, Lydgate looked up and was silent for a moment, like someone woken abruptly from sleep. Then, flushing as the unwelcome situation came back to him, he asked—
“How did you hear that?”
“I visited Mrs. Plymdale this morning. She told me he'd taken the house in St. Peter's Place beside Mr. Hackbutt's.”

Lydgate said nothing. He brought his hands from behind his head and pressed them against the thick hair that, as usual, hung over his forehead, resting his elbows on his knees. Bitter disappointment seized him, as though he had opened a door out of a suffocating room only to find it bricked up. He was also certain that Rosamond welcomed the cause of his distress. He preferred neither to look at her nor to speak until the first spasm of frustration had passed. After all, he thought bitterly, what could a woman care for as much as a house and furniture? A husband without them was ridiculous. When he finally looked up and pushed back his hair, his dark eyes held a miserable emptiness that expected no sympathy. He only said coolly—
“Someone else may come along. I asked Trumbull to keep looking if Plymdale wouldn't take it.”

Rosamond said nothing. She trusted to the chance that her husband and the auctioneer would not speak again until events had justified her interference. In any case, she had prevented the thing she immediately feared. After a pause she asked—
“How much money do those disagreeable people want?”
“Which disagreeable people?”
“The ones who made the list, and the others. How much would satisfy them so they wouldn't trouble you anymore?”

Lydgate studied her a moment as if checking for symptoms. “Well, if Plymdale had paid six hundred for the furniture and the lease, I might have managed. I could have cleared Dover's bill and paid enough toward the others to make them patient, provided we reduced our expenses.”
“But how much would you need if we stayed here?”

“More than I'm likely to get anywhere,” Lydgate replied with a grating edge of sarcasm. It angered him that her mind wandered among impossible wishes instead of facing efforts they could actually make.
“Why can't you tell me the amount?” Rosamond asked, mildly signaling her disapproval of his manners.
“Well,” he said, estimating, “at least a thousand would be needed to put me at ease. But,” he added sharply, “I have to think about managing without it, not with it.”
Rosamond let the matter drop.

The next day, however, she carried out her plan to write to Sir Godwin Lydgate. Since the Captain's visit, he had written to her, and so had his married sister, Mrs. Mengan. Both had expressed sympathy for the loss of her baby and a vague hope of seeing her at Quallingham again. Lydgate had told her these courtesies meant nothing. Secretly she remained convinced that any lack of warmth from his family was caused by his own coldness and contempt. She had answered the letters as charmingly as possible, fairly confident that a definite invitation would follow. Instead, there had been complete silence. The Captain was evidently no great letter writer, and perhaps the sisters had been abroad. Now, however, the season had arrived for thinking of friends at home. In any case Sir Godwin would surely be moved by her appeal. He had chucked her under the chin and compared her to the celebrated beauty Mrs. Croly, who had captivated him in 1790. For her sake he would find pleasure in behaving toward his nephew as he ought. Rosamond was innocently certain of an old gentleman's duty to save her from unpleasantness. She wrote what she considered an exceptionally sensible letter, one that would convince Sir Godwin of her excellent judgment. She explained how desirable it was for Tertius to leave a place like Middlemarch for somewhere better suited to his gifts, how the disagreeable inhabitants had obstructed his professional success, and how he had consequently fallen into financial difficulties from which a thousand pounds would completely free him. She did not mention that Tertius knew nothing of her intention to write. She thought his presumed approval would fit with her account of his great affection for Uncle Godwin as the relative who had always been his best friend. Such was poor Rosamond's skill at strategy now that she applied it to practical affairs.

All this preceded the New Year's Day party. No answer had yet arrived from Sir Godwin. But that morning Lydgate was to discover that Rosamond had canceled his instructions to Borthrop Trumbull. Believing she must gradually get used to the prospect of leaving their house in Lowick Gate, he overcame his reluctance to discuss it again. Over breakfast he said—

“I'll try to see Trumbull this morning and ask him to advertise the house in the ‘Pioneer’ and the ‘Trumpet.’ An advertisement might interest someone who hadn't considered moving. In country towns, people often stay in houses their families have outgrown simply because they don't know where to find another. Trumbull doesn't seem to have had a single inquiry.”
Rosamond knew the unavoidable moment had arrived. “I told Trumbull not to pursue it,” she said with a carefully controlled calm that was plainly defensive.

Lydgate stared, speechless with astonishment. Only half an hour earlier he had been fastening her braids and speaking the affectionate “little language” that Rosamond accepted without returning. She had been like a serene, lovely statue, occasionally rewarding its worshipper with a miraculous dimple. Those feelings still stirred in him, so the shock could not immediately become clear anger; it was a confused pain. He put down the carving knife and fork and leaned back in his chair. At last he said with cool irony—
“May I ask when you did this, and why?”

“When I heard the Plymdales had taken a house, I called to tell him not to offer ours. At the same time I told him to go no further. I knew it would harm you badly if people learned you wanted to give up your house and furniture, and I objected very strongly. I think that was reason enough.”

“So it didn't matter that I'd explained compelling reasons on the other side? It didn't matter that I'd reached a different decision and given instructions to match?” Lydgate spoke bitterly, his brow and eyes gathering thunder and lightning.
Other people's anger had always made Rosamond retreat into cold dislike and become still more calmly correct. Whatever anyone else might do, she was certain she would not misbehave. She answered—
“I think I had every right to speak about something that concerns me at least as much as it concerns you.”

“Certainly you had a right to speak—to me. You had no right to cancel my instructions behind my back and treat me like a fool,” Lydgate replied in the same tone. Then he added with greater scorn, “Can I possibly make you understand the consequences? Is there any point explaining again why we must try to give up the house?”

“You needn't tell me again,” Rosamond said, her voice falling like drops of cold water. “I remember what you said. You spoke just as violently then. But I still think you should try every other means before doing something so painful to me. And advertising the house would, I think, be completely degrading for you.”
“What if I ignore your opinion as you've ignored mine?”
“Of course you can. But before we married, you ought to have told me you'd put me in the worst possible position rather than give up your own way.”

Lydgate said nothing. He tossed his head sideways and the corners of his mouth twitched with despair. Seeing he was not looking at her, Rosamond rose and set his coffee in front of him. He ignored it, continuing an inward drama and argument. Now and then he shifted in his chair, rested an arm on the table, or rubbed his hair. Conflicting thoughts and feelings prevented him either from fully surrendering to anger or from simply holding firm to his resolve. Rosamond used his silence.

“When we married, everyone thought you had such a good position. I could never have imagined you'd want to sell our furniture and move to Bride Street, where the rooms are like cages. If we have to live that way, at least let's leave Middlemarch.”

“Those would be very powerful arguments,” Lydgate said with partial irony. His lips looked pale and shriveled as he stared at the coffee without drinking. “Very powerful, if I didn't happen to be in debt.”

“Plenty of people must have been in debt like this. If they're respectable, people trust them. I'm sure Papa said the Torbits were in debt, and they carried on perfectly well. Acting rashly can't be wise,” Rosamond said with serene authority.

Opposing impulses held Lydgate motionless. Since no argument seemed likely to win her agreement, he wanted to smash and grind some object on which he could at least make an impression, or brutally declare that he was the master and she must obey. Yet he feared more than the effect of such extremes on their life together. He was increasingly afraid of her quiet, slippery obstinacy, which would never let any assertion of power be final. She had also struck one of his most sensitive feelings by suggesting that marriage to him had cheated her with a false promise of happiness. As for declaring himself master, he was not. The resolution he had built through reasoning and honorable pride was already slackening under her numbing touch. He swallowed half his coffee and rose to leave.

“At least I can ask you not to go to Trumbull yet—not until we're certain there's no other way,” Rosamond said. Although she was not easily frightened, she thought it safer to conceal her letter to Sir Godwin. “Promise you won't see him for a few weeks, or without telling me.”
Lydgate gave a short laugh. “I think I'm the one who should demand a promise that you won't do anything without telling me.” He looked sharply at her, then moved toward the door.

“You remember we're dining at Papa's?” Rosamond said, hoping he would turn and give her a fuller concession. Instead he said impatiently, “Oh, yes,” and left. She thought it hateful of him to add an unpleasant temper to the painful proposals he had already made. When she asked so reasonably that he postpone another visit to Trumbull, it was cruel not to reassure her about his intentions. She was certain she had acted for the best in every respect. Each harsh or angry remark from him merely added another offense to her mental record. For months now, poor Rosamond had been associating her husband with disappointment. Marriage, that terribly inflexible relationship, had lost its charm as a source of delightful dreams. It had released her from the disagreeable features of her father's household but had not supplied everything she wished and hoped for. The Lydgate she loved had been, to her, a collection of airy circumstances. Most had vanished, replaced by daily details that had to be lived through slowly, hour by hour. She could no longer float through them by quickly selecting only their pleasing aspects. The demands of his profession, his absorption at home in scientific subjects—which seemed to her almost like a vampire's morbid appetite—and his peculiar opinions on matters never discussed during courtship all steadily estranged her. Even without his placing himself at a disadvantage in the town, even without the first shock of learning about Dover's debt, these influences would have made his company dull. From the early days of her marriage until four months ago, another person's presence had provided pleasant excitement, but that was gone. She would not admit how much the resulting emptiness contributed to her utter boredom. She thought, perhaps correctly, that an invitation to Quallingham and a chance for Lydgate to settle somewhere else—London, or any place likely to offer freedom from unpleasantness—would satisfy her entirely. Then she would not care about Will Ladislaw's absence. She felt some resentment toward him for making so much of Mrs. Casaubon.

This was how things stood between Lydgate and Rosamond when they dined at her father's on New Year's Day. Remembering his temper at breakfast, she appeared mildly indifferent to him. He bore much deeper effects from the inner struggle in which that morning's scene was only one episode among many. His flushed effort in talking to Farebrother, his attempt at the cynical claim that all ways of acquiring money were essentially alike and chance ruled so completely that choice was a fool's illusion, revealed a weakening resolution and a numbed response to his old enthusiasms.

What could he do? He saw even more clearly than Rosamond how dreary it would be to take her to the little Bride Street house, with scant furniture around her and resentment inside her. Ever since poverty had become a threat, life with Rosamond and life with deprivation had seemed increasingly impossible to combine. Even if determination forced those two pictures together, the practical steps needed for the hard change were nowhere in sight. Though he had not given his wife the promise she requested, he did not return to Trumbull. He even began considering a quick trip north to see Sir Godwin. Once he had thought nothing could make him ask his uncle for money, but he had not then experienced the full pressure of still worse alternatives. A letter's effect would be uncertain. Only a meeting, however unpleasant, would let him explain fully and test what family feeling might accomplish. Yet no sooner did he begin to picture this as the easiest course than anger flared again. He had long ago resolved to keep clear of such humiliating calculations, such self-interested worry about the inclinations and pockets of men whose purposes he had proudly refused to share. Now he had fallen not merely to their level but to the level of begging from them.

chapters.title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXV
paragraphs:
One of us two must bowen douteless,
And, sith a man is more reasonable
Than woman is, ye [men] moste be suffrable.
—CHAUCER: _Canterbury Tales_.

Human beings remain slow to answer letters even now, when the general pace of life has quickened. No wonder, then, that in 1832 old Sir Godwin Lydgate took his time over a letter that mattered more to others than to him. Nearly three weeks of the new year had passed. Every day Rosamond waited for a reply to her persuasive appeal, and every day she was disappointed. Knowing nothing of her expectations, Lydgate watched the bills arrive and felt that Dover was about to exercise his advantage over the other creditors. He had never told Rosamond of his contemplated visit to Quallingham. Until the last moment he did not want to admit what she would see as yielding to her wishes after angrily rejecting them. But he really expected to leave soon. By taking the railway for part of the way, he could complete the round trip in four days.

One morning after he had gone out, a letter addressed to him arrived. Rosamond immediately recognized Sir Godwin's hand and filled with hope. Perhaps it contained a separate note for her. Naturally, though, a discussion of money or other help would be addressed to Lydgate. The fact that Sir Godwin had written to him, and even his delay in writing, seemed to confirm that he had fully agreed to her request. These thoughts excited her too much for anything beyond light sewing. She sat in a warm corner of the dining room with the momentous letter on the table before her. Around noon she heard her husband's step in the passage. She hurried lightly to the door and said in her brightest voice, “Tertius, come in. There's a letter for you.”

“Oh?” Without removing his hat, he put an arm around her, turned her gently, and walked with her toward the letter. “My uncle Godwin!” he exclaimed. Rosamond sat again and watched him open it. She had expected his surprise.
As his eyes rapidly scanned the short letter, she saw his normally pale-brown face turn a dry white. His nostrils and lips trembled. He flung the letter down before her and said violently—
“Life with you will be impossible if you keep acting behind my back, opposing me and concealing what you've done.”

He stopped himself and turned away. Then he turned again, paced, sat down, and restlessly got to his feet, gripping hard at the things deep in his pockets. He was afraid of saying something unforgivably cruel.
Rosamond's color changed too as she read. This was the letter—

“DEAR TERTIUS,—When you want something from me, don't send your wife to ask. It's an indirect, wheedling way of going about things that I wouldn't have expected of you. I never care to discuss business with a woman by letter. As for providing a thousand pounds, or even half as much, I can do no such thing. My own family takes every penny. With two younger sons and three daughters, I'm hardly likely to have spare cash. You seem to have run through your own money quickly enough and made a mess of things where you are. The sooner you move elsewhere, the better. But I have no dealings with men in your profession and can't help you find a place. As your guardian I did the best I could, and I let you have your way about medicine. You could have joined the army or entered the Church. Your money would have lasted, and your route upward would have been more certain. Your uncle Charles resents your not choosing his profession, but I don't. I've always wished you well. From now on, however, you must regard yourself as entirely on your own feet.
Your affectionate uncle, GODWIN LYDGATE.”

After finishing, Rosamond sat completely still, hands folded in front of her. She suppressed every sign of her intense disappointment and fortified herself against her husband's anger with silent passivity. Lydgate stopped moving, looked at her again, and spoke with cutting severity—

“Is that enough to show you the harm your secret interference can do? Have you enough sense now to see that you aren't capable of judging and acting for me, of meddling in matters you don't understand and that are mine to decide?”
These were harsh words, but she had thwarted him before. Rosamond neither looked at him nor answered.

“I had almost decided to go to Quallingham myself. It would have been painful enough, but it might have achieved something. Yet there's no point in my making any plan. You're always working against me in secret. You pretend to agree, deceive me, and then leave me at the mercy of your schemes. If you intend to oppose every wish I express, say so openly. Defy me. At least I'll know where I stand.”

It is a terrible moment in young lives when the closeness of love's bond becomes a power to wound. Despite Rosamond's self-control, a tear fell silently and rolled across her lips. She still did not speak, but the calm concealed an intense response. She was so disgusted with her husband that she wished she had never met him. Sir Godwin's rudeness and complete lack of feeling put him alongside Dover and the other creditors: unpleasant people who thought only of themselves and did not care how much they troubled her. Even her father was unkind; he could have done more. In fact, only one person in Rosamond's world escaped blame: the graceful figure with blond braids and little folded hands, who had never spoken improperly and had always acted for the best. “The best,” naturally, meant what she herself liked best.

Lydgate paused, looking at her, and began to feel the almost maddening helplessness that overtakes passionate people when their anger meets innocent-looking silence. Its meek, injured air makes them appear wrong and eventually infects even justified indignation with doubt. To recover the full conviction that he was right, he needed to soften his words.

“Can't you see, Rosamond,” he began again, trying to sound serious without bitterness, “that nothing could be more destructive than a lack of openness and trust between us? Time after time I've expressed a definite wish, and you've appeared to agree, then secretly acted against it. That leaves me unable to know what I can rely on. If you'd acknowledge this, there would be some hope for us. Am I such an unreasonable, raging brute? Why can't you be open with me?” Still she said nothing.
“Will you just admit you were wrong, and say I can trust you not to act secretly again?” he urged. Something pleading had entered his voice, and Rosamond noticed it at once. She replied coolly.

“I can't possibly make admissions or promises in response to the language you've used. I'm not accustomed to being spoken to like that. You've accused me of ‘secret interference,’ of ‘meddling in matters I don't understand,’ and of ‘pretending to agree.’ I've never spoken that way to you, and I think you ought to apologize. You said living with me would be impossible. You certainly haven't made my life pleasant lately. Surely you could expect me to try to prevent some of the hardships our marriage has brought me.” Another tear fell as she finished, and she quietly pressed it away as she had the first.

Lydgate dropped into a chair, feeling defeated. Where in her mind could any protest take hold? He put down his hat, threw one arm over the chair back, and looked down without speaking for a while. Rosamond had a double hold on him: she felt nothing of the justice of his reproach, but keenly felt the undeniable hardships of her married life.
