Her deception about the house had gone further than he knew; she had actually prevented the Plymdales from hearing about it. Yet she had no sense that anyone could rightly call her conduct dishonest. We are no more obliged to classify our own actions rigorously than the ingredients of our food or the materials in our clothes. Rosamond felt wronged, and believed that this was what Lydgate needed to acknowledge.

As for him, the necessity of adapting himself to a nature whose rigidity lay in its refusals gripped him like pincers. He was beginning to foresee with alarm that she might permanently lose her love for him, leaving their life desolate. His emotions were quick and full, so this fear rapidly alternated with the first violence of his anger. Any claim that he was her master would certainly have been an empty boast.

“You haven't made my life pleasant lately”—“the hardships our marriage has brought me”: those words stung his imagination, as physical pain creates an exaggerated dream. What if he fell not only from his highest ambitions but into the hideous chains of hatred at home?

“Rosamond,” he said, turning sorrowful eyes toward her, “you ought to make allowances for what a man says when he's disappointed and provoked. Our interests can't be opposed. I can't separate my happiness from yours. When I'm angry, it's because you don't seem to understand how concealment drives us apart. How could I want to make your life harder by anything I say or do? Hurting you means hurting part of my own life. If you'd be completely open with me, I would never be angry with you.”

“All I've wanted is to stop you rushing us into needless misery,” Rosamond said. His gentler manner softened her too, and tears came again. “It's so hard to be disgraced here among everyone we know and to live so miserably. I wish I'd died with the baby.”

She spoke and cried with the gentleness that makes such words and tears irresistible to an affectionate man. Lydgate moved his chair beside hers and, with a hand both powerful and tender, pressed her delicate head against his cheek. He only caressed her. He said nothing, for what could he say? He could not promise to protect her from the misery she feared: he saw no certain way of doing it. When he left to go out again, he told himself she suffered ten times more than he did. He had a life beyond the house and constant calls to act on behalf of others. He wanted to excuse everything in her if he could. Yet in that forgiving mood he inevitably thought of her as a creature of a different, weaker species. Nevertheless, she had mastered him.

chapters.title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXVI
paragraphs:
’Tis one thing to be tempted, Escalus,
Another thing to fall.
—_Measure for Measure_.

Lydgate had good reason to value the way his practice relieved his private anxieties. He no longer had enough spare energy for independent research or speculative thought. But at a patient's bedside, immediate demands on his judgment and sympathy gave him the extra force needed to draw him out of himself. This was more than the helpful harness of routine that lets foolish men live respectably and unhappy men live calmly. It continually required fresh thought and attention to another person's needs and suffering. Looking back over our lives, many of us would say that the kindest man we have known was a doctor. Perhaps he was the surgeon whose delicate tact, guided by deep understanding, brought help in our hour of need more sublime than any miracle worker's. Some of that mercy, blessing both giver and receiver, always accompanied Lydgate at the Hospital and in his patients' homes. Better than any opiate, it soothed and sustained him through his anxieties and his sense that his mind was deteriorating.

Farebrother's suspicion about opium had nevertheless been correct. When approaching difficulties first began to chafe, and when Lydgate first realized what his marriage would require if it were not to become loneliness in harness—the effort to keep loving without caring too much about being loved—he had tried a dose once or twice. But he had no inherited physical craving for such brief escapes from haunting misery. He was strong and could drink plenty of wine, but felt no desire for it. When other men drank spirits, he took sugar and water, looking with contemptuous pity even on the earliest excitement caused by alcohol. Gambling affected him similarly. He had watched plenty in Paris, observing it as one might a disease. Winning money tempted him no more than drink. He had told himself that the only kind of success worth having must come through a conscious process of difficult, elevated reasoning directed toward a useful result. The power he wanted could never be represented by trembling fingers grasping a pile of coins, or the half-savage, half-idiotic triumph in the eyes of a man sweeping up the stakes of twenty crestfallen companions.

Yet, as he had tried opium, he now began thinking about gambling. He did not hunger for its excitement. Rather, he cast a wistful inward glance at an easy way of obtaining money that required no begging and created no obligations. Had he been in London or Paris, those thoughts, helped by opportunity, would probably have taken him into a gambling house. This time he would not have watched the gamblers, but watched alongside them with the same eagerness. His immense need to win, if chance would only allow it, would have overcome his disgust. An incident not long after the collapse of his airy hopes of help from his uncle showed strongly what a real opportunity to gamble might have produced.

A particular set of men frequented the Green Dragon's billiard room. Most, like our acquaintance Mr. Bambridge, were known as men of pleasure. Here poor Fred Vincy had incurred part of his memorable debt, losing bets and having to borrow from that merry companion. Middlemarch generally knew that substantial sums changed hands there. The Green Dragon's resulting reputation for dissipation naturally made it more tempting in some quarters. Like initiates of Freemasonry, its regulars probably wished they had something more tremendous to keep secret. But they were not a closed society. Plenty of respectable men, old and young, occasionally entered the billiard room to see what was happening. Lydgate had the physical skill for billiards and enjoyed the game. Soon after coming to Middlemarch he had once or twice taken a turn with the cue at the Green Dragon. Later he had neither time to play nor any desire for its company. One evening, however, he had reason to look for Bambridge there. The horse dealer had promised to find a buyer for his remaining good horse. Lydgate had decided to replace it with a cheap hack, hoping the reduction in style might bring him twenty pounds. Every small sum now mattered as a way of keeping his tradesmen patient. Stopping upstairs in the billiard room as he passed would save time.

Bambridge had not arrived, his friend Horrock said, but was sure to come later. Lydgate stayed and played a game to fill the time. That evening his eyes had the peculiar brightness and his manner the unusual animation Farebrother had once noticed. His unexpected appearance attracted plenty of attention among the Middlemarch company. Several spectators, as well as players, were betting eagerly. Lydgate played well and felt confident. Bets fell around him, and a quick thought came that his winnings might double the amount he would save on the horse. He began backing his own shots and won repeatedly. Bambridge arrived without his noticing. Beyond the excitement of play, he was seeing visions of going to Brassing the next day, where gambling took place on a larger scale. Perhaps one powerful snatch at the devil's bait could tear it free of the hook and buy release from his daily demands for payment.

He was still winning when two more visitors entered. One was young Hawley, newly returned from his law studies in London; the other was Fred Vincy, who had lately spent several evenings at his old haunt. Hawley was a skilled billiard player and brought a cool, fresh hand to the cue. Fred, startled to find Lydgate there and astonished at his excited betting, stood back outside the circle around the table.

Recently Fred had been rewarding determination with a little indulgence. For six months he had worked willingly at every kind of outdoor task under Garth. Through rigorous practice he had almost corrected his bad handwriting, though the practice was perhaps less rigorous because he often did it in the evenings at Garth's house under Mary's eyes. During the past fortnight, however, Mary had been staying with the ladies at Lowick Parsonage while Farebrother stayed in Middlemarch carrying out parish plans. Finding nothing more pleasant to do, Fred had gone to the Green Dragon, partly for billiards and partly to savor the old talk about horses, sport, and life viewed from an angle that was not rigorously proper. He had not hunted once that season, owned no riding horse, and had traveled mostly in Garth's gig or on the steady cob Garth could lend him. It seemed a little hard, Fred began to think, to be kept more strictly in harness than a clergyman. “I'll tell you something, Mistress Mary: learning surveying and drawing plans will be harder than writing sermons,” he had said, wanting her to appreciate his sacrifices. “Hercules and Theseus were nothing compared with me. They had sport and never learned a bookkeeper's hand.” Now that Mary was away briefly, Fred had made a small escape, like a strong dog that cannot slip its collar and pulls the chain's staple out instead. Naturally he meant to go neither fast nor far. There was no reason not to play billiards, but he was determined not to bet. His present financial ambition was heroic: to save almost all the eighty pounds Garth offered him and give it back. He could easily do this by abandoning useless spending, since he had more clothes than he needed and paid nothing for his board. Within a year he could repay much of the ninety pounds he had cost Mrs. Garth, unfortunately at a time when she needed it more than now. Nevertheless, on this evening, his fifth recent visit, ten pounds occupied his mind, though it was not in his pocket. It was the amount he intended to keep from his half-year's salary, with the pleasure ahead of taking thirty pounds to Mrs. Garth when Mary would probably be home. He thought of that ten pounds as a fund from which he might risk a little if a promising bet arose. Why not? When sovereigns were flying about, why shouldn't he catch a few? He would never go far down that road again. Still, a man likes to assure himself and his pleasure-loving fellows how much mischief he could do if he chose. If he refrains from making himself ill, ruining himself, or talking as loosely as human limitations allow, it is not because he is a simpleton. Fred did not formulate reasons. Formal reasoning represents very imperfectly the tingling return of old habits and the whims of young blood. But that evening he carried a lurking expectation that once he played he would begin to bet, enjoy a little punch, and generally arrange to feel “rather seedy” the next morning. Actions often begin in such undefined movements.

Almost the last thing Fred expected was to see his brother-in-law looking excited and placing bets just as he himself might. He had never entirely abandoned his old opinion that Lydgate was a prig, overwhelmingly conscious of his superiority. The sight shocked Fred more than his vague knowledge of Lydgate's debts and his father's refusal to help could fully explain. His own desire to join the game abruptly stopped. Their positions had strangely reversed. Fred's fair face and blue eyes, usually bright, careless, and ready for any promise of amusement, had grown involuntarily serious and almost embarrassed, as if at something improper. Meanwhile Lydgate, normally so composed and strong, with an underlying thoughtfulness behind even his sharpest attention, now acted, watched, and spoke with the excited, narrowed awareness of a creature with fierce eyes and retractable claws.

By betting on his own shots, Lydgate had won sixteen pounds. Young Hawley's arrival changed the balance. Hawley made excellent shots himself and began betting against Lydgate's. Lydgate's nervous strain shifted from confidence in his own skill to defiance of another man's doubt. Defiance excited him more, but gave him less certainty. He continued backing himself and began missing frequently. Still he played on. His mind was as completely confined within the steep-sided crevice of the game as that of the idlest ignoramus present. Fred saw him losing rapidly and found himself in the unfamiliar position of racking his brains for a way to interrupt without giving offense, perhaps providing an excuse to leave. Others, he noticed, were also watching Lydgate's strange departure from his usual self. A touch on the elbow and a request for a private word might wake him from his absorption. Fred could think of nothing cleverer than the boldly unlikely claim that he wanted to visit Rosy and wondered whether she was home that evening. He was about to try this desperate, flimsy device when a waiter brought word that Farebrother was downstairs and wanted to speak to him.
Surprised and somewhat uneasy, Fred sent word that he would come at once. With a fresh impulse he went to Lydgate, asked, “Could I have a word?” and drew him aside.
“Farebrother has sent up to say he wants me. He's downstairs. I thought you might want to know, in case you had something to say to him.”

Fred had seized this excuse simply because he could not say, “You're losing horribly and everyone is staring. You'd better leave.” Yet inspiration could scarcely have served him better. Lydgate had not noticed Fred. His sudden appearance, announcing Farebrother, struck like a sharp blow.
“No, no,” Lydgate said. “I've nothing particular to tell him. But the game's over. I must leave. I only came to find Bambridge.”
“He's over there, making a noise. I don't think he's ready for business. Come down to Farebrother with me. I expect I'm in for a scolding, and you can protect me,” Fred added with some skill.

Lydgate felt ashamed, but could not bear to reveal it by refusing to see Farebrother. He went downstairs. They merely shook hands and spoke about the frost. Once the three reached the street, the Vicar seemed quite ready to say goodbye to Lydgate. He clearly wanted to speak to Fred alone. “I interrupted you, young gentleman, because I've urgent business with you,” he said kindly. “Will you walk with me to St. Botolph's?”
It was a fine night, thick with stars. Farebrother suggested taking a longer route to the old church by the London road. His next words were—
“I thought Lydgate never visited the Green Dragon.”
“So did I,” Fred said. “He told me he'd come to see Bambridge.”
“Then he wasn't playing?”
Fred had not intended to disclose this, but now had to answer, “Yes, he was. I suppose it was just by chance. I've never seen him there before.”
“So you've been going often yourself lately?”
“Oh, five or six times.”
“I believe you had a good reason for giving up those visits?”
“Yes. You know the whole story,” said Fred, disliking this catechism. “I told you everything.”

“Which I suppose gives me some right to raise it now. We understand each other, don't we? We're friends who can speak openly. I've listened to you, and you'll be willing to listen to me. May I take a turn at talking about myself?”
“I'm deeply in your debt, Mr. Farebrother,” Fred said, full of uncomfortable guesses.

“I won't pretend you owe me nothing. But I must confess, Fred, that just now I was tempted to undo all that by keeping quiet. Someone told me, ‘Young Vincy is back at the billiard table every night. He won't stand restraint for long.’ I felt tempted to do the opposite of what I'm doing: say nothing and wait for you to climb back down the ladder, first betting, then—”
“I haven't bet anything,” Fred interrupted quickly.

“I'm glad. But my impulse was to watch you take the wrong turn, exhaust Garth's patience, and lose the best chance of your life, the chance you worked rather hard to secure. You can guess what feeling tempted me. I'm sure you know. I'm sure you understand that fulfilling your affections stands in the way of fulfilling mine.”
He paused, apparently waiting for acknowledgment. The feeling audible in his fine voice gave his words solemn weight. But no other emotion could overcome Fred's alarm.
“You couldn't expect me to give her up,” he said after a moment. This was no occasion for pretending generosity.

“Certainly not, when she returned your love. But relationships like these, however long they have lasted, can always change. I can easily imagine your behaving in a way that weakens her attachment. Remember, her commitment to you is conditional. Another man, who perhaps believes he has some claim on her regard, might then win the secure place in her love as well as her respect that you had allowed to slip away. I can quite easily imagine that outcome,” Farebrother repeated emphatically. “A companionship of ready sympathy can outweigh even the longest shared history.” Fred felt that a beak and talons could hardly have made the Vicar's attack crueler than his capable tongue did. A horrible conviction seized him that behind these hypothetical statements lay knowledge of an actual change in Mary's feelings.

“Of course I know it could easily be over for me,” Fred said in distress. “If she's started comparing—” He stopped, unwilling to expose everything he felt, then added with a little bitterness to help him, “But I thought you were my friend.”

“I am. That's why we're here. But I've felt a strong inclination not to be. I've told myself, ‘If that youngster is likely to harm his own prospects, why interfere? Aren't you worth as much as he is? Don't those extra sixteen years of yours, in which you've gone rather hungry, give you more right to satisfaction? If there's a chance he'll go to the dogs, let him. Perhaps you couldn't stop him anyway. Take the benefit yourself.’”

During the pause that followed, a deeply unpleasant chill seized Fred. What came next? He dreaded hearing that something had been said to Mary. This felt more like a threat than a warning. When Farebrother spoke again, however, his tone changed with the encouragement of music moving into a major key.

“But once I intended something better, and I've returned to that intention. I thought, Fred, that hardly anything could help me _hold to it_ better than telling you exactly what I've been feeling. Do you understand me now? I want you to make her life happy, and your own. If there's any chance a warning from me might prevent something that would endanger that, well, I've given it.”

The Vicar's voice dropped at the end. They stood on a patch of grass where the road branched toward St. Botolph's. He paused and held out his hand, as if closing the conversation. Fred felt a new kind of emotion. Someone particularly responsive to a noble act has said it sends a regenerating shudder through the body and makes one ready to begin life again. Fred Vincy was experiencing a good deal of that effect.
“I'll try to be worthy,” he said, stopping before he added, “of you as well as her.” Meanwhile, Farebrother had gathered the impulse to say more.
“Don't imagine I believe her preference for you has weakened at present, Fred. Rest assured: if you keep on the right path, the rest will go right too.”
“I'll never forget what you've done,” Fred replied. “Nothing I can say seems worth saying. Only I'll try not to waste your kindness.”
“That's enough. Goodbye, and God bless you.”

They parted there, but both walked for a long time before leaving the starlight. Much of Fred's thinking could be reduced to this: “Marrying Farebrother would certainly have been a fine thing for her. But if she loves me most, and I'm a good husband?”

Perhaps Farebrother's thoughts could be compressed into a single shrug and a few words. “What a part one little woman can play in a man's life! Giving her up can be a very good imitation of heroism, and winning her can become a discipline.”

chapters.title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXVII
paragraphs:
Now is there civil war within the soul:
Resolve is thrust from off the sacred throne
By clamorous Needs, and Pride the grand-vizier
Makes humble compact, plays the supple part
Of envoy and deft-tongued apologist
For hungry rebels.

Fortunately, Lydgate had finished the evening a loser and left the billiard room with no encouragement to raid the resources of luck. The next day, when he had to pay four or five pounds beyond all his winnings, he felt nothing but disgust with himself. He carried an acutely unpleasant image of the figure he had cut: not merely rubbing shoulders with the Green Dragon's regulars, but behaving exactly like them. A philosopher who takes to betting looks much like a Philistine doing the same. The chief difference appears afterward, in his reflections, and Lydgate found those thoroughly disagreeable to chew over. Reason showed him how a small change of setting might have enlarged the episode into ruin. Had he entered a gambling house, he could have seized chance with both hands instead of picking it up between finger and thumb. Yet although reason strangled his desire to gamble, the feeling remained that, if he could have been sure of winning enough, he would have preferred gambling to the alternative that was beginning to seem unavoidable.

That alternative was an appeal to Bulstrode. Lydgate had boasted so often, to himself and others, that he was entirely independent of the banker. He had supported Bulstrode's plans solely because they let him pursue his own ideas of medical work and public benefit. In their dealings, his pride had been sustained by the belief that he was putting this domineering banker to good social use, despite despising his opinions and often finding his motives an absurd mixture of contradictory impressions. All this had built formidable barriers in his mind against making any substantial request on his own behalf.

By early March, however, his affairs had reached the stage at which men begin explaining that their vows were made in ignorance. What they once called impossible becomes visibly possible. Dover was about to enforce his ugly security. The earnings of Lydgate's practice disappeared immediately into old debts. If the worst became known, suppliers might refuse credit even for daily necessities. Above all, the image of Rosamond's hopeless discontent haunted him. He was beginning to see that he must inevitably stoop to asking someone for help. At first he considered writing to Vincy. But questioning Rosamond confirmed his suspicion that she had already appealed to her father twice, most recently after Sir Godwin's refusal. Papa had said Lydgate must look after himself. “Papa said that one bad year after another had made him trade increasingly on borrowed money, and he'd had to give up many comforts. With his family expenses, he couldn't spare even a hundred pounds. He said you should ask Bulstrode, since you've always been so close.”

Lydgate himself had indeed concluded that if he must finally ask for an unsecured loan, his connection with Bulstrode offered more grounds than any other for a claim that was not wholly personal. Bulstrode had indirectly contributed to the failure of his practice, and had been greatly pleased to secure a medical partner for his projects. Yet who among us has ever fallen into such dependence without trying to believe in claims that make asking less humiliating? Lately Bulstrode did seem to have lost some interest in the Hospital. His health had worsened, though, with signs of a deep nervous disorder. Otherwise he seemed unchanged. He had always been extremely polite, but from the start Lydgate had noticed a distinct coldness toward his marriage and other private affairs. Until now, he had preferred this to any warm familiarity between them. He postponed his intention day after day. His normal habit of acting on a decision had weakened because every possible decision, and the action it required, repelled him. He saw Bulstrode often but used none of these meetings for his private purpose. One moment he thought, “I'll write. Better than talking around the subject.” At another, “No. In conversation I could retreat at the first sign of unwillingness.”

Still the days went by. No letter was written and no special meeting arranged. As he shrank from the humiliation of dependence on Bulstrode, he began growing used to another idea, even less like his remembered self. Of his own accord he considered whether they could follow Rosamond's childish proposal, which had so often angered him: leave Middlemarch without any plan beyond departure. “Would anyone buy my practice even now, for the little it's worth?” he wondered. “Then selling our possessions could be treated as a necessary preparation for leaving.”

He still regarded this course as a contemptible surrender of his present work. It would mean guiltily abandoning a real and potentially expanding field of worthwhile action, to begin again with no soundly chosen destination. A practical obstacle also stood in the way: a purchaser, if one could be found at all, might take time to appear. And afterward? Poor lodgings, whether in the greatest city or the most distant town, would not give Rosamond a life that spared her gloom or spared him the reproach of having brought her to it. A man whose fortunes have reached the bottom of the hill may remain there a long time, however skilled in his profession. In the British climate, scientific insight and furnished lodgings are perfectly compatible. The chief incompatibility is between scientific ambition and a wife who objects to such accommodation.

In the midst of this hesitation, an opportunity settled the matter. Bulstrode sent a note asking him to call at the Bank. The banker had lately shown signs of hypochondria. His sleeplessness was really little more than a worsening of a familiar symptom of indigestion, but he dwelt on it as a warning of approaching madness. That particular morning he wanted Lydgate's advice immediately, though he had nothing new to report. He listened eagerly to the reassurances, which were equally familiar. As Bulstrode received medical comfort, mentioning a personal need seemed easier than Lydgate had imagined. He had been insisting that the banker should spend less time on business.

“We can see how even slight mental strain affects a delicate constitution,” Lydgate said, at the point in a consultation where observations begin to move from the individual to the general, “when we consider how deeply anxiety can mark even someone young and vigorous. I'm naturally very strong, but an accumulation of troubles has shaken me badly lately.”

“I suppose a constitution as vulnerable as mine presently is would be especially liable to cholera, should it reach us. Since it has appeared near London, we have every reason to besiege the Mercy-seat for protection.” Bulstrode did not mean to evade Lydgate's hint. His fears about himself truly absorbed him.

“At least you've done your share in taking practical precautions for the town. That's the best way of asking for protection,” Lydgate said. The banker's religious reasoning, with its muddled metaphors and faulty logic, strongly repelled him, the more so because his sympathy seemed deaf. Still, Lydgate's mind had begun its long-prepared movement toward asking for help and had not stopped. He added, “The town has done well with cleaning and providing equipment. If cholera comes, I think even our opponents will admit that the Hospital's arrangements serve the public.”

“Indeed,” Bulstrode replied somewhat coldly. “As for your recommendation that I reduce my mental labors, Mr. Lydgate, I've been considering a plan of that kind for some time—a very definite plan. I intend at least temporarily to withdraw from directing much of my business, both charitable and commercial. I'm also considering a change of residence. I shall probably close or let the Shrubs and take a house near the coast, with advice, of course, on the healthiness of the location. You would recommend such a measure?”
“Oh, yes,” said Lydgate, sinking back into his chair. He could barely restrain his impatience beneath those earnest pale eyes and that intense self-absorption.

“For some time I've felt I should discuss this with you in relation to our Hospital,” Bulstrode continued. “Under the circumstances I've described, I must naturally give up any personal role in its management. My sense of responsibility does not permit me to continue devoting large resources to an institution I cannot supervise and, to some extent, direct. If I finally decide to leave Middlemarch, I shall therefore withdraw my support from the New Hospital, apart from the lasting support represented by my having paid most of the building costs and contributed further large sums to its successful operation.”

When Bulstrode made one of his customary pauses, Lydgate thought, “Perhaps he's lost a great deal of money.” That seemed the likeliest explanation of a speech that had abruptly changed his expectations. He replied—
“I'm afraid it will be almost impossible to replace that loss to the Hospital.”

“Almost,” Bulstrode agreed in the same slow, silvery voice, “unless the plan changes. The only person we can confidently expect to increase her contributions is Mrs. Casaubon. I've spoken to her about it and explained, as I'm about to explain to you, the desirability of attracting wider support by changing the system.” He paused again, but Lydgate said nothing.

“I mean joining it to the Infirmary. The New Hospital would become a special extension of the older institution under the same governing board. Their medical management would also have to be combined. This would remove the difficulty of providing adequate support for our new establishment. The town's charitable efforts would no longer be divided.”
As he paused once more, Bulstrode lowered his eyes from Lydgate's face to the buttons on his coat.

“No doubt that solves the question of funds,” Lydgate said with an edge of irony. “But you can hardly expect me to welcome it immediately. One of the first consequences will be that the other doctors disrupt or overturn my methods, if only because they're mine.”

“As you know, Mr. Lydgate, I greatly valued the opportunity for new, independent work that you have used so diligently. The original plan was very dear to me, subject always to the Divine Will. But since Providence now calls on me to give it up, I submit.”

Bulstrode showed an exasperating skill in this conversation. The muddled metaphors and flawed reasoning about motives that had aroused Lydgate's contempt could coexist perfectly with a presentation of facts that left him little room to express his disappointment and anger. After thinking quickly, he asked only—
“What was Mrs. Casaubon's response?”

“That is the further point I wanted to explain,” said Bulstrode, who had prepared his official statement thoroughly. “You know how generous she is. Happily, she has—not a great fortune, I presume, but funds she can readily spare. She tells me that although she has set aside most of those funds for another purpose, she is willing to consider taking my place entirely in relation to the Hospital. She would like sufficient time to think it over. I've assured her there is no hurry and that my own plans are not yet final.”

Lydgate nearly said, “If she replaced you, it would be a gain rather than a loss.” But the weight still on his mind checked that cheerful frankness. “Then I suppose I may discuss it with Mrs. Casaubon,” he replied.

“Exactly. That is her express wish. Her decision, she says, will depend largely on what you can tell her. Not immediately, though. I believe she's about to travel. I have her letter here.” He took it out and read: “‘For the immediate future I have another engagement. I'm going to Yorkshire with Sir James and Lady Chettam. What I decide about some land I'm to see there may affect how much I can contribute to the Hospital.’ So there's no need for haste, Mr. Lydgate. I merely wanted to let you know in advance what may happen.”

He replaced the letter in his side pocket and shifted his posture as if their business were finished. Renewed hope for the Hospital only sharpened Lydgate's awareness of the circumstances that poisoned it. If he was going to seek help at all, he must make the effort now, and decisively.

“Thank you for giving me full warning,” he said. His tone was firm, but breaks in his speech showed his reluctance. “My profession matters more to me than anything, and I've regarded the Hospital as the best use I can currently make of it. But the best use doesn't always bring financial success. Everything that has made the Hospital unpopular has also helped make me unpopular as a doctor, along with other causes which I think all arise from my professional enthusiasm. Most of my patients can't pay. I'd prefer them, if I had no payments to make myself.” He waited briefly. Bulstrode merely bowed and continued looking steadily at him. Lydgate resumed in the same broken manner, as though swallowing something he found distasteful.

“I've fallen into financial difficulties from which I can see no escape unless someone who trusts me and my future lends me money without further security. Little of my fortune remained when I arrived. I have no expectation of money from my family. Marriage has made my expenses far greater than I anticipated. At present, a thousand pounds would be needed to put me clear. I mean, to save all my belongings from being sold to meet my largest debt, pay my other debts, and leave a little to keep us ahead on our small income. I've found that my wife's father cannot possibly advance the money. That's why I'm explaining my position to—to the only other man who might be considered personally connected with my prosperity or ruin.”
He hated hearing his own words. But he had spoken, with unmistakable directness. Bulstrode answered without either haste or hesitation.

“I'm sorry to hear this, Mr. Lydgate, though I confess I'm not surprised. Personally, I regretted your marriage into my brother-in-law's family. They have always been extravagant and already owe me a great deal for maintaining their present position. My advice would be to avoid further obligations and a struggle of doubtful outcome. Simply declare yourself bankrupt.”
“That wouldn't improve my prospects,” Lydgate said bitterly, rising, “even if the thing itself were more pleasant.”
“It is always a trial,” Bulstrode replied. “But trials are our lot in this world, my dear sir, and a necessary correction. I suggest you consider my advice.”
“Thank you,” Lydgate said, scarcely knowing his own words. “I've taken too much of your time. Good day.”

chapters.title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXVIII
paragraphs:
What suit of grace hath Virtue to put on
If Vice shall wear as good, and do as well?
If Wrong, if Craft, if Indiscretion
Act as fair parts with ends as laudable?
Which all this mighty volume of events
The world, the universal map of deeds,
Strongly controls, and proves from all descents,
That the directest course still best succeeds.
For should not grave and learn’d Experience
That looks with the eyes of all the world beside,
And with all ages holds intelligence,
Go safer than Deceit without a guide!
—DANIEL: _Musophilus_.

The changes of plan and interest that Bulstrode had either announced or revealed in talking to Lydgate arose from painful experiences since Larcher's sale. That was when Raffles had recognized Will Ladislaw, and the banker had unsuccessfully attempted an act of restitution that might persuade Providence to prevent the painful consequences of his past.

His certainty that Raffles would soon return to Middlemarch unless he died had proved justified. On Christmas Eve he appeared again at the Shrubs. Bulstrode was home to receive him and prevent him from talking to the family, but he could not stop the visit from compromising him and alarming his wife. Raffles was less manageable than on earlier visits. His chronic mental restlessness, worsened by habitual drinking, quickly shook off the effect of anything said to him. He insisted on staying in the house. Weighing two sets of evils, Bulstrode decided this was at least no worse than letting him go into town. He kept Raffles in his private room all evening and took him to bed himself. Throughout, Raffles enjoyed the distress he caused this respectable and prosperous fellow sinner. His jokes presented it as sympathy with his friend's pleasure in entertaining a man who had served him well and had never received everything he had earned. Beneath the noisy humor lay a cunning calculation: he meant to extract a larger payment for releasing Bulstrode from this fresh torture. But his cunning had slightly overshot its mark.

Bulstrode suffered more than Raffles's coarse nature could imagine. He had told his wife he was merely caring for a miserable victim of vice who might otherwise harm himself. Without directly lying, he suggested that a family connection obliged him to do so, and that signs of mental disturbance in Raffles required caution. He would drive the unfortunate man away himself the next morning. He felt these hints gave Mrs. Bulstrode warnings to pass on to their daughters and servants, and explained why he allowed no one else into the room, even with food or drink. Yet he sat in agony, terrified that Raffles's loud, explicit references to the past might be overheard, terrified that his wife might even be tempted to listen at the door. How could he prevent it? How could he open the door to catch her without revealing his fear? She was honest and straightforward, unlikely to stoop to such a method of discovering painful facts. But fear outweighed probability.

Raffles had thus pushed the torture too far and produced an effect he had not intended. By proving himself impossible to control, he convinced Bulstrode that firm defiance was the only remaining course. After putting him to bed, the banker ordered his enclosed carriage for half past seven the next morning. By six he had long been dressed and had spent some of his misery in prayer. If he had used deception or spoken falsely before God, he pleaded his motive of preventing a greater evil. Bulstrode recoiled from a direct lie with an intensity out of all proportion to the number of his less direct wrongs. Many of those wrongs resembled subtle muscular movements of which we are unconscious, though they produce the result we consciously desire. Only what we vividly recognize in ourselves can we vividly imagine Omniscience seeing.

Bulstrode took his candle to Raffles's bedside. The sleeper appeared to be having a distressing dream. Bulstrode stood quietly, hoping the light would wake him gradually and gently; he feared the noise a sudden awakening might cause. For several minutes he watched the shudders and gasps that seemed likely to bring Raffles out of sleep. At last, with a long, half-smothered moan, Raffles started up and stared around in terror, trembling and panting. He made no further sound. Bulstrode set down the candle and waited for him to recover.

A quarter of an hour passed before Bulstrode spoke with a cold authority he had not shown before. “I've woken you early, Mr. Raffles, because the carriage is ordered for half past seven. I intend to take you myself as far as Ilsely. There you can catch the railway or wait for a coach.” Raffles began to answer, but Bulstrode cut him off imperiously. “Be quiet, sir, and listen. I will give you money now, and from time to time I will supply a reasonable amount if you write to ask. But if you appear here again, if you return to Middlemarch, if you say anything that harms me, you will have to live on whatever your malice earns. You will receive nothing from me. Nobody will pay you much for ruining my name. I know the worst you can do and will face it if you dare force yourself on me again. Get up and do as I say, quietly, or I'll call a policeman to remove you. You may take your stories to every drinking den in town, but you won't get sixpence from me to pay for it.”

Rarely in his life had Bulstrode spoken with such tense force. He had spent much of the night weighing this speech and its likely effects. Though he did not trust it to prevent Raffles from ever returning, he had decided it was his best chance. That morning it subdued the exhausted man. Raffles's poisoned system quailed before the banker's cold determination, and he was quietly driven away before the family breakfast. The servants supposed he was a poor relation. They were unsurprised that a strict, proud man like their master would feel ashamed of such a cousin and want him gone. The ten-mile drive beside his hated companion made a dreary start to Bulstrode's Christmas Day. By the journey's end, though, Raffles had regained his spirits and parted contentedly, with good reason: the banker had given him a hundred pounds. Several motives prompted this generosity, and Bulstrode did not closely examine them all. Certainly, while watching Raffles's troubled sleep, he had noticed how much the man had deteriorated since receiving the first two hundred pounds.

He had carefully repeated his firm decision not to be manipulated again. He tried to make Raffles understand that his behavior had made bribing him just as dangerous as defying him. Yet when Bulstrode returned to his quiet home, freed of that repulsive presence, he had no confidence in anything beyond a temporary reprieve. It was like waking from a loathsome dream without being able to shake off its images and their accompanying sensations, as though a dangerous reptile had left slime over everything pleasant in his life.
How can anyone know how much of his innermost life consists of the opinions he imagines others have of him, until that fabric of opinion is threatened with collapse?

His wife's careful avoidance of the subject only made Bulstrode more aware that uneasy suspicions had settled in her mind. He had been accustomed to savoring superiority and complete deference every day. Now the certainty that she watched and judged him with a hidden suspicion of some shameful secret made his voice falter when he offered moral instruction. For anxious people like Bulstrode, anticipating an event can be worse than experiencing it. His imagination continually intensified the anguish of approaching disgrace. Approaching, yes: unless his defiance kept Raffles away, disgrace was certain. He prayed that it would, but scarcely hoped. He told himself in vain that, if allowed to happen, it would be a divine visitation, a chastisement, a preparation. He recoiled from the imagined burning and decided that God's glory would be better served if he escaped dishonor. That recoil finally drove him to prepare to leave Middlemarch. If damaging truths must circulate, distance would lessen the scorching contempt of old neighbors. In a new setting, where his life would not yet have developed the same extensive sensitivities, his tormentor would be less formidable even if he followed. Bulstrode knew permanent departure would hurt his wife deeply, and for other reasons he too would rather remain where he had taken root. He therefore made his early preparations conditional, leaving every possibility open for returning after a brief absence if Providence intervened favorably and removed his fears. On grounds of ill health, he arranged to hand over the Bank's management and relinquish active control of his other local business interests, without ruling out a later return to them. This would add expenses and reduce his income beyond the losses already caused by the general decline in trade. The Hospital stood out as a major expense on which he could reasonably economize.

These were the experiences behind his conversation with Lydgate. Most of his arrangements, however, remained at a stage where he could reverse them if they proved unnecessary. He kept postponing the final steps. Like many a man threatened by shipwreck or a carriage drawn by bolting horses, he clung amid his fears to the sense that something would prevent the worst. Ruining his life by transplanting himself so late might be premature. Besides, it was difficult to explain satisfactorily to his wife why they should go into indefinite exile from the only place she wanted to live.

Among his responsibilities was arranging management of the Stone Court farm during his absence. On this, as on all matters concerning his houses and land in and around Middlemarch, he had consulted Caleb Garth. Like everyone with such business, he wanted the agent who cared more about his employer's interests than his own. Bulstrode wished to retain ownership of the livestock and preserve the option of returning to his favorite recreation of supervision. Caleb therefore advised against relying on a mere farm manager. He should lease the land, stock, and equipment yearly and take a proportionate share of the returns.
“Can I rely on you to find a tenant on those terms, Mr. Garth?” Bulstrode asked. “And will you tell me what annual payment would compensate you for managing the matters we've discussed?”
“I'll consider it,” Caleb replied bluntly. “I'll see how to work it out.”

Without Fred Vincy's future to think of, Caleb probably would not have welcomed more work. As he grew older, his wife continually feared he had too much already. But after leaving Bulstrode, an attractive idea came to him about leasing Stone Court. What if Bulstrode allowed him to install Fred as tenant, with Caleb himself responsible for management? It would be excellent training. Fred could earn a modest income and still have time to learn by assisting with other business. He told Mrs. Garth the idea with such obvious pleasure that she could not bear to dampen it with her constant fear of his taking on too much.

“The boy would be happy enough for two,” Caleb said, leaning back in his chair, his face radiant, “if I could tell him it was settled. Think, Susan! He'd had his mind on that place for years before old Featherstone died. What a lovely turn of events if he ended up there after all, honestly and industriously, because he'd taken to business. Bulstrode might very well let him stay and buy the stock gradually. I can see he hasn't decided whether he'll settle elsewhere for good. I've never been more pleased with an idea. And in time the children could marry, Susan.”
“You won't hint at any of this to Fred until you're certain Bulstrode agrees?” Mrs. Garth asked with gentle caution. “As for marriage, Caleb, we old people needn't hurry it along.”

“Oh, I don't know,” Caleb said, swinging his head to one side. “Marriage tames a man. Fred would need less of my bit and bridle. But I won't say anything until I know where I stand. I'll speak to Bulstrode again.”

He did so at the first opportunity. Bulstrode felt little warmth toward his nephew Fred, but strongly wanted Garth's help with a scattering of business interests on which less conscientious management would cost him heavily. For that reason he raised no objection. He also had another reason to welcome an arrangement benefiting one of the Vincys. Having heard of Lydgate's debts, Mrs. Bulstrode had anxiously asked whether her husband could do something for poor Rosamond. She had been distressed when he explained that Lydgate's affairs were not easily repaired and the wisest course was to let them “take their course.” For the first time she had said, “Nicholas, I think you're always a little hard on my family. I've certainly no reason to disown any of my relations. They may be too worldly, but nobody has ever been able to call them unrespectable.”
“My dear Harriet,” Bulstrode replied, shrinking under her tearful eyes, “I've provided your brother with a great deal of capital. You can't expect me to support his married children too.”
That seemed true. Her protest subsided into pity for poor Rosamond, whose extravagant education she had always expected to bring trouble.

Remembering the exchange, Bulstrode felt he would be glad, when he fully explained his plans for leaving Middlemarch, to tell his wife of an arrangement that might help her nephew Fred. So far he had only said he was considering closing the Shrubs for a few months and taking a house on the south coast.
Garth consequently received the assurance he wanted: if Bulstrode left Middlemarch for an indefinite period, Fred Vincy could become the tenant of Stone Court on the proposed terms.

Caleb was so delighted by the prospect of this “neat turn” of affairs that, without a little loving scolding from his wife to reinforce his self-control, he would have told Mary everything, eager “to give the child some comfort.” He restrained himself, however. He also kept Fred entirely unaware of his visits to Stone Court, where he examined the land and stock more closely and made a preliminary valuation. He certainly pursued these visits more eagerly than the likely pace of events required. But a father's pleasure urged him on. He loved occupying his mind with this possible happiness, held in reserve like a hidden birthday present for Fred and Mary.
“But what if the whole plan turns out to be a castle in the air?” Mrs. Garth asked.
“Well, well,” Caleb answered. “At least it won't fall on anyone's head.”
